Refusals are errors, not empty cards.

OptimizeRoute returns Unavailable when there's no routing connector or no route,
rather than a card with blank measurements. cost_savings is left empty, because
the routing provider returns no cost.
GenerateRoadmap leaves estimated_investment_usd and expected_roi_percent at
zero, which means "not estimated": the roadmap describes a plan, not a
measurement.

Claims and reverse logistics (ClaimsAgentService)
TriageReturnItem is a fixed rule over the condition grade the caller states:



condition_code
Disposition




PRISTINE / A
RESTOCK


DAMAGED / B
REFURBISH


DEFECTIVE / C
RECYCLE


EXPIRED / D
LANDFILL




A missing return_id or condition_code, an unknown grade, or a negative value is
refused with InvalidArgument. An unknown grade is never a decision to destroy
stock.
estimated_recovery_yield_usd, refurbishment_cost_usd and routing_destination
aren't derived, because FACE holds no pricing, cost or facility data for returns.
basis_note says so on every response.

Reverse-logistics outcomes that rest on records are produced as
RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence documents. See
Evidence documents.
Reading the results

A simulation is a model's reasoning over grounded context. It isn't a measured
outcome, and its confidence is the model's own.
The results cover only the scenarios that ran. Read the counts before
treating the results as covering the estate.
Passing validation means the rules are consistent. It doesn't mean the scenario
will happen.
A compared option is scored over the rows the run read. A recommendation means
its range cleared the others on that sample, not that it will work.
A triage disposition follows the stated grade, not an inspection. It's only as
good as the grade the caller supplied.

docs/concepts/compliance-finance-operati.title: Compliance, finance, operations
docs/concepts/compliance-finance-operati.body:
Compliance, finance, operations

You open the Compliance, Finance and Operations views from the Remediation
links on Actionable Twins. Each runs its own analysis and lists what it found, with
a remediation order for each finding. You address an order to a department, set a
standing route for a category, and record the decision. Orders still waiting for a
decision are also listed in the Waiting for you lane on Actionable Twins. The
business rules behind the findings, and the policy you set on each, are on Why.
Three services share one request and response shape:



Service
RPC




ComplianceService
AnalyzeCompliance


FinanceService
AnalyzeFinance


OperationsService
AnalyzeOperations



Each takes an AnalyzeComplianceRequest (system_context) and returns an
AnalyzeComplianceResponse with these fields:

compliance_status: Pass, Warning, Fail, or Unable to Assess.
violations (ComplianceViolation): the category, severity, description, related
rule and remediation for each finding.
audit_trail.
spoken_response.
orders: remediation orders (see below).
live_data_note.

How a verdict is produced
The compliance agent assesses the instance's configuration and the session context sent with the request.
Configuration values are labelled as declarations. A value an operator asserted is not treated as evidence that a control is implemented.
No usable answer means no verdict. When an assessment cannot be made, the status is Unable to Assess with the reason, and the failure is audit-logged.
live_data_note says which live data was read. A current server always sets it.
The verdict rests on the session context sent with the request and on the instance's
own configuration, and the note tells the reader so.
Remediation orders and the workflow
A RemediationOrder is the dispatchable form of a finding. It's shaped like an
evidence document: a subject, facts read from records (specifications), coded
determinations, citations, deadlines, ordered steps, and a seal written at
approval.
An order's steps and deadlines come from cited records, and the department is set by a person or by your routing rule.
Order ids are stable (the rule id plus the subject), so an operator's routing and
decision survive the next analysis. The operator's half of an order is stored apart
from the derived half and merged when the order is read:
How a derived order reaches a decision:

An order starts NOT_ROUTED.
Did an operator address it?
AssignRemediation → OPERATOR_ASSIGNED.
If not, is there a routing rule for its category?
SetRemediationRoute → OPERATOR_ROUTING_RULE.
If not, it stays NOT_ROUTED.




From any of those three states, DecideRemediation resolves the order to DRAFT / APPROVED / REJECTED / SENT.

AssignRemediation addresses one order to a department and contact. The server
records assigned_by from the verified session, and ignores any author fields the
client sends.

SetRemediationRoute, ListRemediationRoutes and DeleteRemediationRoute
manage a standing table. The table maps a finding category, matched exactly, to a
department. An order routed by the table says so (OPERATOR_ROUTING_RULE), which is
distinct from a person addressing that particular order. A person's assignment always
takes precedence over a rule.
DecideRemediation records the human decision (RemediationDispatch). An empty
state means nobody has decided yet, which is not the same as DRAFT. decided_by
is the verified subject. FACE sends nothing by itself. SENT records something a
human did outside the platform, and channel records how.

RemediationAssignment.basis takes one of these values:



basis
Meaning




DERIVED_FROM_RECORD
The provider was named on a cited record.


OPERATOR_ASSIGNED
A person addressed this order.


OPERATOR_ROUTING_RULE
A standing category rule addressed it.


NOT_ROUTED
The default. An unaddressed order is addressed to nobody, not to everybody.



An empty orders list is a valid response. The overlay and routing apply to whatever
orders the analysis produced.
Rules
RulesService serves the rules that the rules-reconciliation agent recognises in the
data. You see them on Why, each with its policy drawer:

ListRules, AnalyzeCode and CheckCode read.
UpdateRulePolicy sets only the operator-owned enforcement posture (RulePolicy),
from the policy drawer. It can't edit the agent's findings (name, logic, proposed
code or reconciliation_status). An operator who could overwrite a finding could
make FACE agree with them. Saving a posture also re-runs the compliance and
twins agents (see
Agents & oversight).

Reading the results

A Pass is the model's reading of the context it was given. Read
live_data_note for what that context was.
Operator declarations are claims about the environment, not controls the system
has verified.
An order with an assignment has not necessarily been sent. Only a recorded
SENT dispatch says a person sent it.

docs/concepts/twin-ontology/.title: Twin ontology & graph
docs/concepts/twin-ontology/.body:
Twin ontology & graph

FACE models an operation as a twin graph: entities (a site, a dock, a reefer trailer, a
sensor) and the relations between them, each fact stamped with where it came from, how it is
known and when it was true. The vocabulary is GS1 EPCIS 2.0 + CBV 2.0: every class and relation maps to an EPCIS
role, as the tables below show.

The ontology (classes, relations, validators, URI forms) is served by TwinOntologyService (GetTwinOntology, ValidateTwinIdentifier).
The graph is Runink's twin store (append-only, bitemporal) on FACE's appfs tenant root, served by
TwinGraphService (ListTwinEntities, GetTwinEntity, TraverseTwin, UpsertTwinEntity,
LinkTwinEntities, ListTwinDevices).
In the FACE app, the twin lives on Actionable Twins › Map. The Entities panel over
the map is the entity browser (filter by class, search). The map plots located entities as
points, and tapping one opens its detail. A device connection's card on Ask opens the
devices that connection reported into the twin.

Classes
Every identifier property is optional. An entity whose GLN or SSCC is not known has none; FACE
never pads, derives or guesses one.



Class
Key (scheme)
EPCIS / CBV role




Site
GLN (AI 414)
bizLocation / readPoint, urn:epc:id:sgln:….0


Facility
GLN
bizLocation


Dock
SGLN (GLN + AI 254 extension)
readPoint / bizLocation (sub-location)


Zone
SGLN
bizLocation (sub-location)


YardSlot
SGLN
bizLocation (sub-location)


Vehicle
GIAI (AI 8004)
epcList / parentID


Trailer
GIAI
epcList / parentID


Container
ISO 6346 (BIC)
epcList / parentID, urn:epc:id:bic:…


LogisticUnit
SSCC (AI 00)
epcList / parentID


Asset
GIAI
epcList


ReturnableAsset
GRAI (AI 8003)
epcList / parentID (serialised GRAI only)


Device
GIAI
sensorMetadata.deviceID


Sensor
GIAI
sensorReport (type, uom, minValue/maxValue)


Shipment
GSIN (AI 402)
bizTransactionList (desadv, bol)


Order
none (issuer's number)
bizTransactionList (po)


Lot
LGTIN (AI 01 + AI 10)
quantityList, ilmd (cbvmda:lotNumber, expiry)



Quantities carry UN/CEFACT Recommendation 20 unit codes, as EPCIS does: CEL (°C), KGM,
MTR, MTK, P1 (percent), SEC, DD (degree). The full property list per class, with
required/optional and the EPCIS field each maps to, is what GetTwinOntology returns.
Relations
Each relation is directed (from rel to), and the ontology lists which class pairs it allows.
A write outside that domain/range is refused.



Relation
Example
EPCIS




locatedIn
Trailer → YardSlot
ObjectEvent, bizLocation; bizStep arriving / receiving / storing, ended by departing


isPartOf
Dock → Facility, Sensor → Device
master data (the SGLN hierarchy; sensorMetadata.deviceID)


measures
Sensor → Trailer
ObjectEvent with sensorElementList; bizStep sensor_reporting


carries
Vehicle → Trailer → Container
AggregationEvent, parentID = carrier; loading / unloading


assignedTo
Trailer → Dock, Device → Trailer
none: a plan, not an observation; maps to bizTransaction or master data


fulfils
Shipment → Order
shared bizTransaction (po + desadv/bol) on the shipping event


containedIn
LogisticUnit → LogisticUnit, Lot → LogisticUnit
AggregationEvent (childEPCs or childQuantityList); packing / unpacking



Lots are produced by EPCIS TransformationEvents.
Identifiers
ValidateTwinIdentifier accepts a plain key, a GS1 element string ((414)…(254)…), an EPC URI
or a GS1 Digital Link, checks it (GS1 mod-10 check digits; ISO 6346 mod-11) and returns its other
forms. The FACE app's identifier field calls it on every edit: the server is the only place a check
digit is computed, and a server it cannot reach reads not checked, never valid.
The EPC URI needs the GS1 Company Prefix length, which a plain key does not carry. When the
caller does not supply it, the EPC URI is reported absent with that reason, and the twin stores the
Digital Link instead. It is never formed from an assumed split, because a wrong split is a
well-formed URI naming another company's object.
The validators are tested against the published examples of the GS1 EPC Tag Data Standard 2.1
(§7), for instance urn:epc:id:sscc:9521141.1234567890 ↔ (00)195211412345678900, and against
the ISO 6346 code CSQU3054383.
Example: a DC with a reefer at the door
The keys below use GS1's example company prefix 9521141 from the Tag Data Standard. They show
the shape, not a real site.
Site       "DC Nord"          gln  = urn:epc:id:sgln:9521141.12345.0
Dock       door "7"           sgln = urn:epc:id:sgln:9521141.12345.D7     isPartOf → Site
YardSlot   slot "Y12"         sgln = urn:epc:id:sgln:9521141.12345.Y12    isPartOf → Site
Trailer    plate "AB-123-CD"  giai = (absent: not known)                  locatedIn → YardSlot Y12
                              trailer_type = reefer                       assignedTo → Dock 7
Device     reefer logger      giai = urn:epc:id:giai:9521141.LOG42        assignedTo → Trailer
                              heartbeat_every_s = 300
Sensor     return-air probe   measurement_type = gs1:Temperature          isPartOf → Device
                              uom = CEL, spec_min = 2, spec_max = 8        measures → Trailer
LogisticUnit pallet           sscc = urn:epc:id:sscc:9521141.1234567890   (carried by) Trailer

The trailer's GIAI is absent because nobody stated one. The graph still knows the trailer, by
its plate and by its relations.
Evidence and the device registry
Every fact carries an evidence kind from a closed vocabulary, strongest first:
OPERATOR_CONFIRMED, OBSERVED, DECLARED, INFERRED, GUESSED. Edits made in the FACE app are
OPERATOR_CONFIRMED with source operator:. A session that names no person is refused,
and nothing is recorded as anonymous. Writes need the editor or admin role.
ListTwinDevices judges each Device and Sensor against its heartbeat_every_s:

Reporting: it was heard from within that interval.
Device fault: it missed its heartbeat, or was never heard from after the first interval.
Awaiting first report: it is new and its first heartbeat is not due yet.
Not judged: no interval is stated, so its silence cannot be judged.

None of these states is shown as "all fine".
Site plans in the twin
A factory or warehouse plan (IFC, DXF, PDF or a picture; IFC and DXF are BIM/CAD plan files) is shown
on Actionable Twins › Map, in the Site plans panel over the map: the values inferred from
the plan, with their twin bindings. The map draws its footprint for physical-storage awareness,
and tapping the footprint opens the plan over the map. A plan becomes part of the twin only
through an operator. When an editor or admin confirms a zone, a dock or a yard slot,
FACE writes it to the twin graph:

a Zone, Dock or YardSlot per confirmed element, named after the element (its
door number or slot label for a dock or a slot), with evidence OPERATOR_CONFIRMED, source
siteplan:: (the element id carries the IFC GlobalId or the DXF handle)
and the person who confirmed it in x_confirmed_by. Its level, outline (x_polygon, in plan
units), position, width and area (x_area_m2: the area the file states, else computed from the
outline when the plan's unit is known) are kept as x_ properties;
the plan's Site and Facility, named after the plan and written once. Facility, zones
and docks are isPartOf it; a yard slot is part of the Site.

Elements read from a file but never confirmed, and everything the vision model proposed, are
never written. Identifiers are not derived from a plan: an SGLN appears only when an operator
enters it on the twin entity, and a later re-confirm keeps it. Confirming again or editing the
element writes a new version of the same entity. Rejecting it, or changing it to a kind with
no twin class, writes a tombstone, but only if it was bound before. A kind change between
zone, dock and yard slot retires the old entity and writes the new one.
Both sides link to each other. The site plan on the map shows the selected element's
twin entity and opens its detail; the entity's detail names the plan and element it came from
and opens the plan on that element.
The plan's live overlay places a reading on a zone when its location names the zone, and also
when the reading's sensor is a Device that is locatedIn a zone the plan bound, or a
Sensor that isPartOf such a device. The reading says which rule placed it: zone id,
zone name, or twin locatedIn (with via  for a sensor). A sensor whose twin names two
of the plan's zones is not placed.
Reading the results

Operators build the graph, directly or by confirming site-plan elements. An empty
twin is shown as empty.
A GIAI is checked for form. GIAI has no check digit, so a well-formed GIAI can still
be a mistyped one.
Supply the GS1 Company Prefix length to form an EPC URI. A plain key does not carry
it, and without it the EPC URI is reported absent with that reason.

docs/concepts/vision/.title: Vision & CCTV
docs/concepts/vision/.body:
Vision & CCTV

FACE grades what a camera sees with the sovereign vision tier: whether a pallet, crate
or container door is damaged, how badly, and what it's made of. The camera surface is
SurveillanceService, with two paths that answer different questions.



RPC
Path
Purpose




IngestSurveillanceFeed
Graded. A pushed frame, or frames sampled from an RTSP/HTTP feed.
Grades the subject, with optional detection.


DetectLiveFrame
Live. One validated frame.
Quick boxes on a live view. No grade.


GetEvidenceFrame
Fetches the annotated frame an ingest retained.
Shows what was assessed.



Camera connections are set up on Settings › Integrations, as described in
Data sources. A camera connection's card on Ask opens its live
view, with the feed already chosen.
The graded path

Frame grading. FACE grades the inspectable subject in the frame: the object,
its material, a damage_grade (PRISTINE, DAMAGED, DEFECTIVE or
DESTROYED) and an estimated damage_percentage.
A person is not a subject. If the frame holds no inspectable object,
subject_object is empty, and every grade field is a no-finding, not a low
score. People never appear in objects.


Per-object results. objects (DetectedObject) lists every inspectable object
with its own box. class_vocabulary names the label set in use (for example
runink.coldchain.v1). label_in_vocabulary is optional: when it's absent, the
label wasn't checked.
Instance detection. This step is off by default. When it is switched on,
FACE returns one box per instance of the graded class, and frames_detected
reports how many frames were looked at.
When a live detector has already boxed the graded objects one instance at a
time, this step is skipped, and detection_note says so.



Where each box came from
DetectedObject.box_origin (BoxOrigin) names the stage that produced each box:



BoxOrigin
Source




VISION_GRADING
The grading step. The weakest source, because grading answers at scene level.


VISION_DETECTION
The instance detection step.


REGION_CLUSTERING
Region proposals: geometry only, with no label or grade.


LOCAL_DETECTOR
The live detector.



A box from the live detector carries detector_label, detector_label_set and an
optional detector_confidence. These fields are informational. Material, grade and
damage figures come only from the grading step.
Notes that explain an absence
Three response fields explain gaps. An empty object list is also what a correctly
empty yard looks like, so these fields are how a reader tells the cases apart.

localisation_note: why findings arrived without boxes.
detection_note: what the live detector did. It is never empty.
evidence_note: why no annotated frame was retained. Retention is off unless an
operator sets a window.

Coordinates

Coordinates are normalised. Every box on the wire is 0 to 1 of the frame's width
and height, so a client can draw it at any size.
Frames are resized before grading. The 0 setting disables resizing. Leave the
default unless support asks you to change it.

The live path
DetectLiveFrame returns boxes for one frame, quickly. Its response has no field
for a grade, percentage, material or classification, so a live call never carries a
verdict.
detection_latency_micros reports the processing time per frame. It isn't a
round-trip time or a frame rate.
A live call is not stored as a result. It writes no evidence frame or sighting.
Aggregating sightings
MaterialAnalyticsService.AnalyzeMaterialQuality folds graded ingests into
distributions by material, class and damage grade over a time window:

Every count is a count of sightings, meaning one object in one frame in one
ingest. It is never a count of things.
Ungraded is not pristine. Ungraded sightings are counted separately.
A comparison needs a baseline window. A delta appears only when a baseline
window is supplied.
corpus_scanned and corpus_durable say whether data was actually read and
whether it survives a restart.

Reading the results

A grade and a damage percentage are estimates from the image. They aren't a
physical inspection.
A box may not be on the right object. detection_note reports which stage ran,
not whether it was correct.
A retained evidence frame shows the reviewer what was assessed. It isn't a
forensic artefact.

docs/concepts/agents-and-oversight/.title: Agents & oversight
docs/concepts/agents-and-oversight/.body:
Agents & oversight

FACE's agents draft; a person decides. Nothing an agent proposes is sent, filed or
paid until a named person approves it on Actionable Twins, and FACE recommends an
option only when it is clearly better on the data.
The agents are driven by one orchestrator, the Ralph loop. What
an agent may do is bounded by guardrails on its input, a review of the actions it proposes, and a human decision before anything is adopted.
The Ralph orchestrator
RalphOrchestratorService.ExecuteLoop runs an agent loop (thought, then action, then
observation) and streams each step back as an ExecuteLoopResponse:

agent_id picks the template, for example twins, hypothesis or rules_recon.

LoopStatus reports progress: WORKING, EXECUTING, OBSERVING, DONE, FAILED
or MAX_REACHED.

On DONE, judgements carries the reviewer's verdicts.

The same loop drives the scenario simulations behind Options and the interactive
twin (StreamTwins).
Agent templates
The loop serves these agent templates: twins, hypothesis, rules_recon,
ai_posture, compliance, finance, claims, claims_leakage, fraud_detection,
fulfilment, reverse_logistics, route_twin, predictive_maintenance, telemetry,
documentation, vision, voice, cop and self_healing.
Other analyses, such as the market and due-diligence passes, run outside the loop.
Tools
The loop can dispatch three tools, each authorised against the caller's verified identity:



Tool
Tier
What it does




read_file
read
Reads a file from a confined path. Output is truncated.


run_sql
write
Runs a read-only query against the connection the loop was started with.


delegate_to_claims
invoke
Hands a sub-task to the claims agent.



Agents that run on their own
No one picks an agent and presses Run. The server runs the agents a change makes stale,
for the tenant it happened in:

A rule's enforcement posture is saved (RulesService.UpdateRulePolicy, from the
policy drawer on Why): compliance and twins run.
A scenario is simulated (SimulateScenario or InteractiveSimulate): twins
runs, to turn the outcome into proposals.

Changes made close together are combined into one run per agent. These runs are named auto:, and Options
shows the ones in flight in one line (nothing at all when none is running). What they
propose still waits for a person on Actionable Twins.
Guardrails (OpenBias)
Before a prompt reaches the model, FACE checks it against guardrail rules. The rules cover each service's entry points, GenerateSOP, GenerateRoadmap, TriageReturnItem and camera-feed grading included. Every refusal is audited.
Review of proposed actions 
Every proposed action is independently reviewed before a person decides. The reviewer's verdict is shown on the card. An action the
review does not support is not offered for approval, and one that was not reviewed is
shown as not reviewed, never as accepted.
Human-in-the-loop points
A person makes these decisions. The server records who made each one, from the
verified session:



Decision
Where
RPC
What's recorded




Send an option for approval
Options
HypothesisService.SendToTwins
The option, its figures as the server computed them, and the approval it needs. Sending decides nothing.


Approve or reject an action card
Actionable Twins
TwinsService.ExecuteAction
decision_trail. A reason is required on rejection. Approval seals the evidence document. A two-person card needs two different named people.


Make an approved decision a standing rule
Actionable Twins, on an approved card
TwinsService.ProposeStandingRule / ApproveStandingRule
Proposer and approver; the approver must be an org admin who is not the proposer.


Address a remediation order
Actionable Twins and its remediation views
ComplianceService.AssignRemediation
assigned_by and assigned_at_unix


Standing routing rule
The remediation views
SetRemediationRoute
set_by and set_at_unix


Decide a remediation order
Actionable Twins and its remediation views
DecideRemediation
decided_by and decided_at_unix


Set a rule's enforcement posture
Why, the rule's policy drawer
RulesService.UpdateRulePolicy
The operator-owned half only. It can't change findings.


Read actual customer rows
API only; the FACE app does not call it
ConfigService.SampleConnectionDataset
A separate, bounded call. Exploring a source never samples it. See Data sources.



Nothing FACE derives is sent, filed or settled without one of these decisions. Where an
action does execute, for example an email draft through a connected account, its
outcome is reported per artifact in not_executed. See
Action cards & money.
Reading the results

Guardrails make misuse harder; they don't make it impossible. A prompt fence
makes injection harder, and it does not solve it.
A review is a second opinion. A supporting verdict does not show the action is
right.
Recording a human decision is not enforcing it. The recorded decision shows who
approved what. It doesn't show that they reviewed it carefully.

docs/architecture/.title: Architecture
docs/architecture/.body:
Architecture

FACE is a Go gRPC backend and a Flutter web cockpit that runs on the Runink
platform layer. The platform layer ships with FACE (you do not buy Runink TIDDE, Trusted Intelligence for Developer & Data Experience, separately) and
supplies the shared services FACE relies on: the TLS edge, the inference plane, the
service mesh's certificate authority, the key that encrypts FACE's data at rest, and the
object store. Each customer gets its own FACE instance.
The path a request takes (each FACE instance serves one customer):

Browser (the FACE cockpit) → Platform TLS edge, over HTTPS.
Edge → Frontend, which serves the app and proxies its calls.
Frontend → Control plane (the gRPC services), over gRPC-web on the same origin.
Control plane →
Inference plane (text · vision · voice), over HTTP;
Sealed storage, per tenant;
a Managed runner over mutual TLS → your data sources; and
a Self-hosted runner in your network over mutual TLS → data sources behind your firewall.



Components



Component
What it does




Frontend
Serves the Flutter web app and passes its calls (gRPC-web, sign-in and API paths) to the control plane on the same origin, so the app needs no backend address baked in.


Control plane
The FACE gRPC backend: runs, briefs, analysis, options, the twins and their decisions, follow-ups, remediation, camera and sensor feeds, and the other services in the API reference.


Managed runner
A FACE process that reads your data sources on the platform. It is the default runner for every connection. Fetches always run on a runner, never on the control plane.


Self-hosted runners
Runners you run in your own network, so reads happen close to the data. A runner enrols with a single-use setup ticket and dials out to FACE; nothing dials in to it. See Runners.


Inference plane
Language, vision and voice models behind an OpenAI-compatible HTTP interface. FACE ships no model server and refuses to start without the plane's address. See Sovereign models.


Storage
FACE's encrypted file tree (sessions, users, connections, schedules, run records) and append-only logs for traces, decisions and data lineage. Every object is sealed under a per-tenant key and bound to its path. See Encryption.



The pipeline
A question on Ask, or a brief, starts a run: fetch → extract → reason → recommend.

Fetch. A runner reads the connected sources, through allowlisted, read-only
queries. More than thirty connection types are supported; see
Data sources.
Extract. The rows are profiled and clustered, and the estate's domains, rules
and data health are assessed.
Reason. Agents work over the extracted context in a reasoning loop,
behind guardrails. FACE
tests the scenarios your estate suggests.
Recommend. The twins turn the findings into action cards. A card needs an approval before anything is carried out, and every decision is recorded. See
Agents & oversight.

Instances and access
Each FACE instance serves one organisation. Only accounts Runink has approved for that
instance can sign in, and each carries one role. See
Access and the trial.
Where your data goes

Model calls stay with the inference plane. Prompts, retrieved records and model
outputs go only to the plane the deployment configures, never to an outside AI
service. On a trial, or when Runink runs FACE for you, that plane runs on Runink's
machines and your data is processed there; when you host FACE, it runs where you do.
Outbound calls go only to what you connect. That means your data sources, plus
the web searches, messaging and email channels you configure. FACE calls no paid map
or geocoding service.
Credentials are separated from configuration. A connection record has no field that
can hold a secret. Credentials go to a sealed credential store and are never returned
through the API.
At rest, data is encrypted under a key derived from the key-encryption key the
platform provides. FACE refuses to start without it rather than fall back to
plaintext.

Details and limits are in Security & trust. Where FACE
can run is in Deployment.

docs/architecture/security/.title: Security & trust
docs/architecture/security/.body:
Security & trust

This section describes the security controls FACE implements. It is written for
the security reviewers, assessors and architects who have to decide whether FACE
can hold their data.
Every page follows the same rule. It describes a control that exists in the code,
names the setting, RPC or error text the control uses, and ends with the scope of the control: what it covers, and what stays with your
deployment. If a property is not stated here, do not assume
FACE has it. Ask us instead.

Note: FACE is SOC 2-oriented in its design. These pages do not claim any
certification, attestation or authorisation: SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001,
FedRAMP, CMMC or ITAR. See Compliance posture for what that
wording means and what it does not.

Design principles

Fail closed at startup. FACE will not start without its mesh certificate
authority, its at-rest key-encryption key, its session signing key, its
encrypted application root and an inference endpoint. No fallback mode runs
with any of these missing.
No switch that turns a control off. Mesh mTLS, at-rest sealing and the
instance-metadata refusal cannot be disabled by any environment variable.
Sovereign inference. FACE calls no outside AI service. Text, vision and
speech recognition go to the inference endpoint the deployment configures,
and FACE links no AI vendor SDK.
The lineage log records structure, never values. It records which source
was read, what shape came back and where it went. It never records the data
itself.
Say what a control does not do. A green check is worth only what it
actually proves.

Pages in this section

Defence in depth: Authenticated, role-checked requests, mesh mTLS with rotating ECDSA identities, no plaintext downgrade.
Identity & access: Sessions, OIDC, MFA, allowlists, RBAC, and the exact unauthenticated surface.
Encryption at rest: Envelope encryption, the required KEK, sealed metadata, objects and credentials.
Sovereign inference: Platform-run models, no third-party LLM API, and where data does leave.
AI safety: Prompt fencing, OpenBias guardrails, the voice line, review of proposed actions.
Auditability & lineage: Always-on audit events, and an observed lineage log that carries no data values.
Network egress controls: Encrypted connectors only, the connector address policy, read-only SQL checks, and IPv6-first dialling.
Compliance posture: What SOC 2-oriented means here, and why the compliance env vars are declarations.

Where the platform ends and FACE begins
FACE runs on the Runink platform layer, which ships with FACE: you do not buy Runink TIDDE (Trusted Intelligence for
Developer & Data Experience) separately. The platform provides the edge that terminates browser TLS, the mesh
certificate authority, the envelope key, the object store and the inference plane.
These pages describe what the FACE backend enforces itself, together with the shared
libraries it links. Where a property depends on how the platform is deployed, the page
says so. Where FACE runs is covered in Deployment.

Warning: Scope of this section. It describes the code. It is not a
penetration test or an audit report, and it says nothing about the deployment
you run. Network policy, log retention, key custody and backups all belong to
your installation, and you have to verify them there.

docs/architecture/security/zero-trust/.title: Defence in depth
docs/architecture/security/zero-trust/.body:
Defence in depth

FACE layers independent checks rather than relying on any one of them. Every
user request carries an authenticated session and passes a role check (see
Identity & access). Services also authenticate each other
with short-lived, rotating ECDSA certificates issued from a shared cluster
certificate authority.
Service-to-service: mesh mTLS
Mesh mTLS is unconditional
When the backend starts, it builds a rotating TLS identity from the shared mesh
CA, which the platform supplies to FACE as a secret and rotates.
If it is missing, unreadable
or expired, the process stops with
mesh identity unavailable, refusing to start and does not serve.
No environment variable produces a plaintext mesh connection. There is no
"mTLS off" setting, and no code path falls back to an insecure transport.
That identity secures:

FACE server to runner. The FACE server (the control plane) uses it to dial a
runner, and that call carries connector credentials and tenant data.
Raft consensus peers. The raft service replicates configuration, runner
and connection metadata between nodes.
Mesh gRPC. It is the transport for every peer that dials FACE's gRPC
services as a mesh member.

Rotating, short-lived ECDSA leaves
Identities come from Runink's shared PKI library (the pki.Source type):



Property
Value
Where it is set




Key type
ECDSA P-256
the shared PKI library


Leaf lifetime
1 hour
LeafTTL: time.Hour


Re-issue interval
every 20 minutes
RotateEvery: 20 * time.Minute


Minimum TLS version on mesh hops
TLS 1.3
pki ServerConfig / ClientConfig


Server-side client authentication
tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert against the mesh CA
pki.Source.ServerConfig



The re-issue interval must be shorter than the leaf lifetime, and pki refuses
any configuration where it is not. A leaf is replaced well before it expires.
Leaves can never outlive the CA that signed them, and the process readiness
check tracks both leaf validity and CA validity. A pod whose mesh identity has
lapsed reports itself not ready instead of continuing to answer health checks.
TLS 1.3 limits every mesh cipher suite to an AEAD construction (AES-GCM or
ChaCha20-Poly1305). It also rules out renegotiation and static-RSA key exchange,
and encrypts the handshake.
Chain verification, and what identity means
A mesh server requires a client certificate and verifies it against the mesh CA
during the TLS handshake. A peer without a CA-signed certificate is rejected
before any RPC is dispatched.
A mesh client verifies that the server's certificate chains to the mesh CA,
with the server-authentication key usage. On the mesh, identity means "holds a
leaf signed by this cluster's mesh CA". It does not mean "is this particular
hostname". That lets peers be dialled by service name, pod address or IP without
re-issuing certificates. It also means the CA private key is the root of trust
for the whole mesh, and its custody is a platform responsibility.
No plaintext downgrade
A failed handshake means a failed call: the caller receives Unavailable with
the x509 reason. FACE does not retry in plaintext and does not come up with a
degraded transport.
Tests pin this behaviour:

TestRunnerDialDoesNotDowngradeToAPlaintextRunner and TestRunnerDialFailsClosedOnCASkew dial a real plaintext-only runner and a
runner holding a certificate from a different CA. It requires both to be
refused. A positive control proves each refusal came from the TLS layer and
not from a dead port. TestRunnerRefusesAnAnonymousCaller makes a real
anonymous TLS dial and requires the mutual half of mTLS to reject it.
TestNoInsecureTransportInAnyPackage parses every Go source file in the
repository and fails on insecure.NewCredentials, grpc.WithInsecure, ALTS
credentials or InsecureSkipVerify: true. It also fails on
InsecureSkipVerify set from a variable. The only places it excuses are the
MQTT and Kafka connectors, which read the connection's insecure_skip_verify
field. No stored connection can turn that field on: the connector security
policy refuses any connection with it set, on write and on every read (see
Network egress controls).
Because the parse skips comments, prose that mentions these names can neither
trip the check nor satisfy it.

Consensus is never served without mTLS
The raft service carries no user token, so it is exempt from bearer
authentication (see the unauthenticated surface).
To keep that exemption safe, the raft service is served only on the mTLS
peer listener, never on a plain registrar.
TestRaftServiceIsNeverOnTheApplicationListener walks every non-test file in the
command package and fails if any code registers the raft service anywhere else.
People: the browser path
Browser traffic reaches FACE through the platform's edge, which
terminates the browser's TLS. The edge dials the FACE control plane's TLS
sidecar with a cluster-CA client certificate, and the sidecar forwards to the
application port. With that sidecar in place the backend binds
to loopback, so the application port listens on loopback only;
a bind host that is not an IP literal stops the backend at startup. A separate
health listener serves only /livez, /readyz and
/auth/config so the kubelet can probe the pod. FACE does not ask a browser
for a client certificate, because a browser cannot present a mesh identity.
Because the sidecar delivers edge traffic over loopback, FACE never treats a
loopback address alone as proof that a caller is local.
Every user request instead has to carry a session bearer token, which the auth
interceptor validates on every call. A verified mTLS identity is recorded on the
request as an attribute, but it never replaces a session token.
TestAVerifiedMTLSPeerStillNeedsABearerToken pins that rule.
Transport identity on the request
FACE never trusts a header that claims a certificate was checked upstream. The
caller's transport identity is read only from TLS state that this process
negotiated. A certificate counts only if the TLS stack populated its verified
chains. A certificate that was merely presented does not count.
That identity is used in three places:

Server reflection (the gRPC service catalogue) is available only to a
verified mTLS peer. Anyone else receives
server reflection requires a verified mTLS peer.
The internal model service. ModelService answers without a session only
when the caller is this process: a loopback peer that also holds a verified
mesh certificate (see
Identity & access).
The policy subject. When a verified certificate is present, its common name
is attached to the policy subject as the attribute mtls_client_cn.

Typed request identity
After a token is verified, the tenant, role, subject and subscription tier go
onto the request context under an unexported, typed key. No other package in
the process, dependencies included, can collide with those keys or forge them.
TestNoBareStringContextKeysInPackageCmd fails on any context.WithValue in the command
package whose key is a string. The security policy engine reads a typed
policy.Subject built from the same verified values. That subject's
internal-system flag is always false for a remote caller. Only an in-process
audit hook sets it to true.

Warning: Scope of these controls

Mesh mTLS covers service-to-service connections only. It puts no
client-certificate requirement on browser traffic. User requests are
authenticated by session tokens, and they are only as strong as the session
controls described in Identity & access.
The mesh CA is managed by the platform. Protecting the CA key, and distributing and
rotating the CA, is done by the platform, not by FACE.
Envelope encryption applies at rest; TLS applies in transit. Data is
sealed before it is written, as Encryption at rest
describes. Confidentiality in transit comes from TLS.
The tests cover FACE's own dial and listen code only. They say nothing
about the certificates your cluster actually holds. Check CA validity on your
own installation.

docs/architecture/security/identity-acce.title: Identity & access
docs/architecture/security/identity-acce.body:
Identity & access

Every gRPC call to FACE passes through one of two interceptors, AuthInterceptor
(unary calls) or StreamAuthInterceptor (streaming calls). Both live in
the backend's authentication interceptor and apply the same rules. Only the short list of
methods below runs without a session token.
Sessions

The token is opaque and random. A session token carries 256 random bits,
base64url-encoded. The client never decodes it. The server keeps only the
token's SHA-256 hash, in FACE's encrypted application root, together with the
role, email and tenant it recorded at sign-in. None of those values come from
the client.
Every request is validated. The interceptor looks the token up in the
session store on every call, reading through a cache that is at most 2 seconds
old. A missing, unknown, revoked or expired token is refused with
invalid or expired session token. A request with no token is refused with
authorization token is not provided.
Lifetime. Sessions last 12 hours. A service-account key is a session
issued for 365 days.
A slow store is not a sign-out. If the session store does not answer in
time, the call fails with Unavailable (the session store did not answer;
try again), not Unauthenticated, so the app retries instead of signing the
person out.
Revocation. Logout ends every session of the signed-in subject, as well as
the bearer that made the call. The subject is taken from the verified request
context, never from a token in the request body. Changing or deleting an
account ends that account's sessions, because a session carries the role it
was issued with. A revocation on any replica is honoured by every replica and
runner within the 2-second cache window, and
TestARevokeOnTheControlPlaneIsRefusedOnARunner tests exactly that.
The signing key is required. A deployment-supplied signing key signs the short-lived MFA
challenge. FACE refuses to start without it and never generates one. A key
generated per process would differ between replicas.

Sign-in methods
IdentityService/Login takes three methods: a password (CREDENTIALS), the
second step of a password sign-in (MFA_VERIFY), and an OIDC ID token
(GOOGLE_OIDC).
Password, with TOTP

Passwords are stored as bcrypt hashes.
If the account has TOTP enrolled, a correct password does not issue a
session. It returns STATUS_MFA_REQUIRED and a signed MFA challenge that
expires after 5 minutes. A session is issued only after a valid TOTP code
arrives with that challenge. TOTP verification accepts one 30-second step of
clock skew either way.
A deployment can require TOTP. A deployment setting names all, or a
comma-separated list of roles (admin, writer, reader). A covered account
with no TOTP enrolled is not signed in by its password alone: Login returns
STATUS_MFA_ENROLMENT_REQUIRED with a fresh secret, and the session is issued
only once the person has added it to an authenticator and entered a code. A
value FACE does not understand stops the backend at startup. Unset, empty or
off means no requirement.
The break-glass admin. A deployment may define one break-glass administrator
account, which FACE creates or updates with the admin role at every startup.
Without that configuration no break-glass admin exists; FACE never invents one.
When a deployment allows Google sign-in only, password sign-in is refused (Password sign-in
is disabled — use Google sign-in) for every account except the break-glass
admin.

OIDC single sign-on
SSO is enabled when the deployment configures an OIDC issuer and client ID. The issuer
can be any standards-compliant OpenID provider. FACE verifies the ID token itself
against that issuer using Runink's shared OIDC verifier, so no identity
broker sits in between.
Verifying who someone is does not decide whether they may enter:

The token must carry an email address with email_verified true. Otherwise
the result is SSO verification failed.
The allowlist fails closed. AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS lists who may sign in
through SSO. If SSO is configured and the allowlist is empty, nobody can
sign in through SSO (SSO is not available on this instance), and the
operator gets a specific log line explaining why. A verified identity that is
not on the list is refused with
This account is not authorized for this instance.
The role comes from the instance's own grant. On every SSO sign-in FACE
reads the access grant for that email from its own instance (the users the
Admin page edits) and records that role. An email the grant does not list, or
whose grant has lapsed, keeps the role it already has. If the grant cannot be
read, the sign-in is refused rather than given a guessed role.
A first-time allowed user with no grant is given a local account with the
lowest role (Reader) and a random password. That password is never derived
from the OIDC subject, so password sign-in cannot become a predictable way
into an SSO account.
The allowlist is re-checked on every request, not only at sign-in, so
removing an address from AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS refuses that person's next
request. Runners do not hold the list: they accept the caller only as
dispatched by the control plane over verified mesh mTLS.
With TOTP, FACE checks the second factor only for password sign-in. For SSO
the second factor belongs to the identity provider.

Public bootstrap values
GET /auth/config tells the FACE web app how to sign in. It returns exactly
four fields and nothing else: google_client_id (the public OIDC client ID),
oidc (whether SSO is configured), declared_variant (the operator-declared
deployment variant, standard when unset) and recaptcha_site_key. No secret
ever passes through this endpoint.
reCAPTCHA is not enforced on FACE, and nothing on
these pages depends on it. The backend keeps an optional check that stays off
while its settings are unset, and they are unset on every FACE deployment.
With the check off,
recaptcha_site_key is empty and the app loads nothing from Google.
Roles and authorisation
A session's stored role is mapped through the shared role vocabulary, and the
mapping fails closed:



Stored role (accepted spellings)
FACE role
Policy tier




admin, org_admin, owner
ROLE_ORG_ADMIN
Admin


writer, editor
ROLE_WRITER
Writer


reader, viewer
ROLE_READER
Reader


service, service_account, svc
ROLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT
Reader


anything else, including empty
none: the request is refused
none



An unrecognised role never falls back to a default. The request is refused with
this account's role is not recognised on this instance, so it grants no access.
Beyond the role, the interceptors enforce the following:

Service accounts cannot manage the instance. A service account is refused
on configuration, activation, identity and access-management methods with
RBAC: Service Accounts cannot perform management actions. It keeps the
reads a runner needs: ListRunners and ListConnections.
In the policy engine it holds the Reader tier, so it cannot drive the
agent loop's write-tier tools.
Licence and subscription checks fail closed. If a signed (Ed25519) licence
is configured, it takes precedence over the tenant registry. An invalid or
expired licence refuses every call with license expired or invalid.
Features restricted by subscription tier are refused with a
PermissionDenied error.
Tenant scoping. The verified tenant is the only tenant a handler may act
on. A handler that accepts a tenant ID in its request has to compare it with
the verified one. The service-account key issuer does exactly that and refuses
with cannot issue a service account for another tenant. Only an
organisation admin can issue service-account keys.
Scoped tokens stay scoped. The token FACE mints for a carrier's media
socket is refused as an API credential
(this token is scoped to the media socket and cannot be used for API calls)
and refused on the WebRTC signalling endpoint.

The unauthenticated surface
This is the complete list of gRPC methods that skip session authentication.
TestAuthExemptionsAreOnlyTheApprovedSet parses both interceptors and fails if any other
method reaches its handler with no further check. The same test fails if one of
the two gated entries below loses its gate.



Method (prefix)
Why it has no session token
What protects it instead




/semantics.v1.IdentityService/Login
A caller cannot present a session before it has one.
The credential, MFA and SSO checks described above.


/semantics.v1.ActivationService/ValidateLicense
The licence key is itself the credential.
It returns a single boolean: whether the key is an Ed25519-signed licence within its validity window.


/semantics.v1.RaftService/
Consensus peers carry no user token.
Served only on the mesh mTLS listener. See Defence in depth.


/semantics.v1.ModelService/
The backend dials its own model service.
This process only: a loopback caller that also presented a verified mesh certificate. Any other caller gets ModelService is served to this process only (loopback + verified mesh mTLS). The one exception is GetModelStatus, which the app polls to show whether inference is ready; it is not exempt and needs a session like any read.


/grpc.reflection.
Debugging tools carry no user token.
Verified mTLS peers only. Loopback alone is not enough, because the edge delivers browser traffic over loopback. Any other caller gets server reflection requires a verified mTLS peer.



A small set of plain-HTTP routes sits on the same server:



Route
Authentication




GET /auth/config
Public by design. It returns only the four public fields listed above.


GET /readyz, GET /livez
Public, so the kubelet can probe them. They return check names and pass/fail results.


/api/map/basemap/, /api/map/glyphs/
Public. They serve the basemap tiles and glyphs the deployment configures, and answer 404 when none is configured.


/twilio/voice, /twilio/message, /comms/twilio/status
A valid carrier request signature is required, checked against the deployment's Twilio auth token or the one an admin set. With no token, the endpoint refuses every request (503) rather than accepting unsigned ones. Inbound messages are accepted only from senders that resolve to a known contact.


/twilio/stream
A short-lived signed token (10 minutes) in the stream URL FACE generated, checked before the WebSocket upgrade.


/oauth/mail/callback
No session, by design: it completes a mailbox connection, and the single-use OAuth state names which one.


POST /webrtc/signal
A session bearer token, verified exactly as on the gRPC path.



The voice line is the one prompt path a person can reach without an account,
since it sits behind a phone number. The controls on that path are described in
AI safety.

Warning: Scope of these controls

Session authentication is the authentication for user traffic. A verified
mTLS peer identity is recorded as an attribute, never accepted in place of a
session (TestAVerifiedMTLSPeerStillNeedsABearerToken). Account hygiene
(strong passwords, TOTP enrolment, a tight SSO allowlist) therefore bears the
full weight of user authentication.
MFA covers password sign-in. TOTP is enforced for every account that has
enrolled, and a deployment setting makes enrolment mandatory for the roles it
lists. SSO sign-in relies on the identity provider's own second factor.
One instance serves one customer. Sessions and accounts are
deployment-wide, and each customer gets its own FACE instance. The boundary
between customers is the instance, not per-request routing inside one
instance.
Revocation takes up to 2 seconds to reach every replica. It is prompt,
but not instantaneous.
Typed context keys prevent collisions, not false values. The identity on a
request is exactly as trustworthy as the session check that produced it.

docs/architecture/security/encryption/.title: Encryption at rest
docs/architecture/security/encryption/.body:
Encryption at rest

FACE encrypts what it persists before it is written. It does this with one
envelope scheme, from Runink's shared envelope-encryption library, under one
key-encryption key (KEK) that the platform supplies. FACE does not start without
that key.
The envelope scheme
Every sealed value is an independent envelope:

A fresh random 32-byte data-encryption key (DEK) is generated for each seal.
The plaintext is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under that DEK.
The DEK is wrapped with AES-GCM under a key derived from the KEK.
The wrapped DEK, the nonces and the ciphertext are stored together, so one
envelope is self-describing.

FACE writes the scheme's version 2 format everywhere it seals. That covers
the encrypted application root (and the metadata tables inside it) and the
object store. Each of those writers opts in to version 2 in code, not through a
setting.
Version 2 adds the following:

A per-envelope wrap key. The KEK never keys AES-GCM directly. Each
envelope wraps its DEK under
HKDF-SHA256(KEK, salt, "runink/envelope/v2/wrap") with a fresh 256-bit
salt. No GCM key ever encrypts more than one message, so no per-key message
budget needs tracking.
A key identifier. Each envelope carries an 8-byte key ID derived from the
KEK by HMAC. Opening selects the right key directly, and a blob sealed under an
unknown key says so. The ID reveals nothing about the key.
An authenticated header. The version, key ID, salt and nonces are all
covered by the GCM tag, so they cannot be edited or spliced between envelopes.
Context binding (AAD). The caller's additional authenticated data is bound
in last. FACE uses it to tie each ciphertext to where it lives, so a sealed
blob copied to another key, table or path fails to open. It is not merely
hidden there.

Key rotation
The KEK is a 32-byte key the platform delivers to FACE as a secret.
To rotate it, the platform publishes the new key and moves the old
one into a retired-key slot. Existing envelopes still open because
the key ID selects the retired key. Because only DEKs are wrapped by the KEK,
rotation never requires re-encrypting bulk data. A retired key stays in
the retired-key slot until the shared store's reseal tool has rewritten
everything sealed under it.
A required KEK

Mounting the encrypted application root needs the KEK. Without it FACE stops,
because that root holds the session store and a process without it could
authenticate nobody.
The backend exits specifically on envelope.ErrKEKUnavailable, and its log
line names the missing key. Opening a legacy
face.db without the KEK is fatal for the same reason.

No code path runs FACE with sealing switched off, and there is no setting that
switches it off.
Where sealing applies
The encrypted application root
FACE's sessions and application metadata live in its own appfs root, from
Runink's appfs library, mounted at the backend's application root:

An app-specific key. The root's key is
HKDF-SHA256(KEK, info="runink/appfs/face"). A key or blob leaked from another
Runink application opens nothing of FACE's, even on a shared object store.
Path-bound blocks. The AAD of every block includes the application and the
block's full path, tenant segment included. A block moved to another path,
tenant or application fails to open.
Two backends. With an object store configured, the root is a scoped view of
the object store. Without it, the root is appfs's encrypted local backend,
in a local data directory. FACE has no in-memory mode.

The root holds sessions, user accounts, the compute-budget ledger and, under
tenants//, everything the customer configured or produced:
connections and their credentials, application metadata, fetch snapshots,
briefs and personas, remediation overlays and routes, rule policies, and call
transcripts.
Application metadata tables
FACE keeps no database of its own. Its application metadata (accounts,
schedules, operator overlays, fetch snapshots, compute budgets and the
application-metadata record) is a set of append-only tables inside the appfs
root above, so every object they write is sealed in the version 2 format under
FACE's derived key and bound to its full path. There is no plaintext mode.
A runner keeps its own state the same way, in its own tables under the tenant
(tenants//var/lib/runners..*), not on its image layer.
FACE no longer uses SQLite. An
instance upgraded from an older build may still have its old face.db file. At
startup FACE imports its rows once into the appfs tables, opens it only if it
exists, and never writes to it again.
The object store
The object-store client from the shared store library seals every object it
writes with the same envelope scheme (version 2), bound to its bucket and key.
FACE's durable records go through it: the appfs root itself when
an object store is configured, the observed lineage records, the fetch run
history, and (when an object store is configured) the tenant's indexed knowledge.
Credentials
Connector credentials get stricter handling than any other data FACE holds:

A connection record cannot hold a secret. The connection type in
the connection record has no field a secret would fit in. When a connection
arrives over the wire, the connection translator lifts every
secret-named field (password, client secret, API key, token, service-account
JSON) into a separate credential bundle. The secret-bearing fields in the wire
schema are read on the way in and never written on the way out. A client that
reads a connection back gets them empty.
Credentials are sealed rows, not files. Each credential bundle is a row in
FACE's appfs connections table, sealed under FACE's derived key and bound to
its path.
Credentials are not replicated through consensus. Only connection metadata
goes through the raft log. Credential bundles do not.
Credentials never come from the server's environment. A connector reads
its credentials only from its own connection's sealed bundle, never from the
backend's process environment. A person enters them in Settings ›
Integrations › Systems in the FACE app. The quickstart data sources
Runink hosts are registered from a connection manifest that cannot carry a
credential: each
password is read from a named variable at registration time and stored
sealed, without being printed.
Local files are owner-only. Where FACE writes local files (credential
compatibility paths, and the knowledge corpus when no object store is
configured), directories are created 0700 and files 0600.
TestKnowledgeCorpusIsNotWorldReadable writes real corpus content through the
real code path, then checks every file and directory mode.
The inference service token is never invented. The configured service token is the
only source of the token FACE presents to the inference plane. FACE never
generates a fallback, and TestFaceNeverInventsAServiceToken guards that.


Warning: Scope of these controls

Sealing at rest and encryption in transit are separate layers. Sealing happens before a
write. Where a sealed payload crosses a network, it is ciphertext because it
was sealed for storage, not because of any transport decision. Transport
confidentiality comes from TLS (see Defence in depth).
Key custody belongs to the platform. Whoever holds the KEK can
open everything sealed under it. Generating, storing, distributing and
rotating that key happens outside FACE.
Re-sealing does not reach old copies. The reseal tool rewrites live
objects. It does not rewrite copies that already exist in older backups, or a
legacy face.db an upgraded instance still keeps. Removing those is an
operator step.
File modes are not encryption. 0600/0700 protects local files from
other users on the host. It does not protect them from the host's
administrator or from someone who has the disk.

docs/architecture/security/sovereign-inf.title: Sovereign inference
docs/architecture/security/sovereign-inf.body:
Sovereign inference

FACE calls no outside AI service. Every model request FACE makes for text,
vision and speech recognition goes to the inference plane the deployment
configures, a mistral.rs server run by the platform. Prompts, fetched records
and model answers never go to a model vendor.
How inference is wired

One endpoint. All text generation, vision grading and agent
reasoning are HTTP calls to the inference plane. The base URL comes from one deployment setting, the only one
FACE reads for it. The vision and voice tiers can be pointed at their own
endpoints. When those are unset, both fall
back to the main endpoint.
No bundled model server. FACE ships no inference binary and starts no
model-server child process. It has no local "fallback" model tier.
Inference is required to start. If the inference endpoint is unset or
blank, the backend refuses to start with an error saying no inference endpoint is configured.
If a call reaches a model client with no endpoint, it fails with
FailedPrecondition naming the missing setting, rather than a transport error that
names nothing.
An authenticated plane. FACE presents the configured service token
to the plane. It never generates a token of its own.
Internal-only model service. FACE's own ModelService gRPC door, which its
agents use to reach the plane, accepts only this process (loopback plus a
verified mesh certificate). The one method the app calls, GetModelStatus,
says only whether inference is ready and needs a session. See
Identity & access.
Speech. Phone-call transcription is a request to the plane's voice tier.
Speech synthesis runs in process with a bundled local engine (Piper), so
generating audio does not leave the pod.
No LLM vendor SDK. FACE's Go module does not depend on any LLM vendor SDK,
and the backend uses no LLM orchestration framework.

What sovereign means for data egress
Keeping inference in the cluster removes the largest egress path an AI product
usually has. It does not mean FACE never talks to the outside world. These
are the paths that can leave your network, and each one exists only if you
configure the feature behind it:



Path
What leaves
When it exists




Data-source connectors
Queries and API requests to the source systems you connect: warehouses, ERPs, logistics APIs, devices.
For each connection you create. The destinations are governed by the connector address policy.


Web search and page reading
Search terms and page requests to the public web, fetched through a headless browser.
When an agent or the FACE app uses web search or reads a web page.


Maps and routing
Nothing. FACE calls no map, places, geocoding or routing service: routes are computed in the cluster, basemap tiles are served by FACE itself, and place lookups are ordinary web search (the row above).
Never.


Single sign-on
Token verification against your OIDC issuer.
Only when single sign-on is configured.


Email
Drafts the twins agent creates in a connected mailbox. A person reads and sends them; mail a model composes is never sent without a person.
Only with a connected mailbox (see AI safety).


Telephony and messaging
Call audio and messages carried by the telephony provider, Twilio.
Only when the voice line or messaging is configured.



Everything a model reads (fetched rows, page text, call transcripts) is
processed by that inference plane. The table above lists the only routes by
which data leaves.

Warning: Scope of these controls

A configured endpoint is not a reachable plane. The startup check
confirms that the inference endpoint is set. It dials nothing, and it does not
prove a model is loaded.
Sovereignty depends on where the plane runs. FACE sends inference to the
URL it is given. That the URL points at a plane the platform runs, and not at
an outside service, is a deployment fact, and you have to verify it on your
own installation.
Voice calls go through a carrier. A phone call's audio travels through the
telephony provider before it reaches FACE. Transcription and reasoning are
sovereign, but carriage of the call is not.

docs/architecture/security/ai-safety/.title: AI safety
docs/architecture/security/ai-safety/.body:
AI safety

FACE's agents read a customer's records and propose actions. The controls on
this page sit at the points where untrusted text reaches a model, and where a
model's output could turn into an action. None of them makes a language model
safe against a determined adversary. Together they make attacks harder and
bound what an attack can achieve, and each one says where it stops.
Two kinds of untrusted text
FACE treats text a caller types differently from content the platform
fetched, because the two carry different risks.
Caller commands: screened before any model call
FACE screens every prompt in layers before it reaches a model. A prompt that is
refused never reaches the model, the caller is told it was refused, and the
refusal is audited.
Fetched content: fenced as untrusted data
Connector rows, page text, OCR output and earlier model answers derived from
them are wrapped by ai.FenceUntrusted before they reach a prompt:

Instruction. The model is told explicitly that the fenced block is
untrusted data to analyse, that it carries no authority, and that
instructions inside it are part of the data and must never be obeyed.
An unguessable delimiter. The fence markers are drawn fresh and at random
for each call, so content cannot close its own fence.
No bytes changed. The content appears verbatim, so legitimate records are
not mangled.

OpenBias guardrails
Each agent service has guardrail rules that ship with the backend. A matching rule
refuses the request with PermissionDenied and writes a PROMPT_REJECTED audit
record, with the actor ID hashed.
The rules cover security abuse (such as prompt injection and attempts to tamper
with the audit trail) and bias and ethics (such as discriminatory decisions).
The agent loop
The agent loop (ExecuteLoop) runs only agents that have guardrails. A request for any other agent is refused with a FailedPrecondition.
The voice line
The phone line is the one prompt path a person can reach without an account.
Every caller utterance is screened before any model is called.
A refusal is spoken to the caller as a sentence. It is not an error, because
an error on this path would be silence on the line. Refusals are audited.
The carrier's webhooks require a valid request signature, and the media socket
requires a short-lived token that FACE minted. See
Identity & access.
Review of proposed actions
Every proposed action is independently reviewed before a person decides. The reviewer's verdict is shown on the card.

An unsupported action is not offered. It is kept only as a record with
accepted=false, and never served as a recommendation.
"Not reviewed" is never shown as agreement. An action that was not reviewed is
marked as such and is never silently accepted.
The verdicts stay in FACE. No verdict is written to another platform's store.

Bounding what agents may do
A mitigation against injection has to be paired with limits on what model
output can cause:

Agent email is always a draft. An email an agent composes is created
as a draft in the operator's mailbox for a person to read and send; no agent
sends mail on its own, whatever the agent email allowlist
or the decision-authority policy says (see Auditability & lineage).
Both are still evaluated, and the draft is audited with the recipient hashed,
so the record shows what the policy would have allowed.
Proposed actions are bounded. Every action an agent proposes is checked
against that agent's allowlist of action kinds and approver roles and its
OpenBias rules before it is shown, high-risk action kinds (such as moving
money) are refused for every agent, and links to hosts outside
the deployment's allowed output hosts are removed from answers. Nothing an agent proposes
runs until a named person approves it. The one exception is self-healing of
FACE's own runtime (restarting a runner, tripping a circuit breaker,
scaling, rolling back), which runs automatically,
behind its own fixed list of actions and a kill switch.
Tool gating. Agent tools are authorised through the security policy
engine, against the verified subject of the request. A service-account token
holds the Reader tier and cannot reach write-tier tools.
Read-only SQL. Agent-issued and user-issued SQL both go through the same
read-only check as every other query. See
Network egress controls.


Warning: Scope of these controls

Indirect prompt injection is an unsolved problem. Fencing makes injection
materially harder. The real limit is what output is allowed to do, which is
why the controls above cap agent actions.
Guardrails reduce risk; they do not remove it. Tests prove the rules
fire. They do not prove the rules catch every harmful request.
A review verdict is a second opinion. It is a check, not proof. Keep a
human in the loop for consequential actions.

docs/architecture/security/audit-lineage.title: Auditability & lineage
docs/architecture/security/audit-lineage.body:
Auditability & lineage

FACE keeps two different records. The audit log records security-relevant
events: who did what, and which control refused what. The lineage log records
data movement: which source was read, what shape came back and where it went.
Neither record contains the data itself.
Audit logging
Always on
Audit logging is always on. The environment variable ENFORCE_AUDIT_LOGGING gates nothing (see
Compliance posture). Records are not dropped silently.
What a record contains
Each audit record is structured JSON with a timestamp, an event type, an actor
ID, a target ID and a details map.

Actor and target identifiers are hashed with SHA-256 before they are
written. The hash is deterministic, so an assessor can still group events by
actor without the log exposing the raw identifier. The system actor SYSTEM
is recorded as is.
Refusals are recorded. Guardrail refusals include the rule ID, severity,
category, compliance tags and the action PROMPT_REJECTED. Voice-line
refusals record the reason and the control that fired, but never the caller's
words. An agent email downgraded to a draft records the recipient only as a
hash.

Where records go
FACE writes audit records to its standard output as structured JSON, beside its
OpenTelemetry-shaped application logs. The platform's log pipeline collects them
from there.
Request logging
The unary request interceptor logs only the method name and the request size in
bytes. Request bodies are never logged, because they carry prompts, data rows
and document content. Personal data is masked before it is written to logs and
audit records.
Decision authority and the decision log
How much authority an action needs
Before an approved action runs, FACE checks how much authority it needs. Depending on the
kind of action, its value and its risk, a card asks for one named approver, two different
named approvers, or can only be advice that is rejected rather than approved.
Actionable Twins shows each card's tier, the rule IDs that decided it and why. A card that needs two approvals shows "1 of 2 approvals" and who approved, and a card that
cannot be approved shows no approve control. The server enforces this whatever the client shows.
A deployment can set its own approval policy. Nothing a model proposes leaves the platform
without a person approving it, and mail the agent composes is drafted in the operator's mailbox for a person to read and send.
The decision log
Every decision is recorded in a decision log, with who decided, the card, the
policy that applied and the outcome. Admins can read the log, and check its integrity,
on the Admin page opened from Settings › Account. If a decision cannot be recorded,
the action does not run.
Observed data lineage
The lineage recorder captures observed data movement, one immutable record
per event. It does not describe lineage from a schema. It records reads that
actually happened.
Where it is captured

Every tabular connector. extractors.ConnectorForType returns every
connector wrapped in a lineage decorator. All connectors are covered with no
per-connector code.
Camera ingests. Frames pushed by a camera do not pass through the connector
seam, so the ingest path records them itself: one record per ingest on every
return path, failures included.
Deliveries. The connector does not know where its result will go, so the
calling pipeline attaches the destination afterwards. It does so only on the
branch where the rows actually landed.

What a record contains
A lineage record carries structure only. Every field is an identifier, a
structural name, a count, a duration or a fingerprint:



Field group
Contents




Kind
extraction (a source was read), delivery (a result landed somewhere) or discovery (a source described its own catalogue, and no business data moved)


Source identity
Connection ID, connection name, connector type, environment, runner. Taken from the connection's labels only, never from its configuration or credentials.


What was asked
A literal-free query shape plus its fingerprint


What came back
Column names and a row count


Outcome
ok, empty or error. An error is kept as a closed-set error class plus a SHA-256 fingerprint of the driver message. The message itself is never stored.


Destination
Kind, ID and name of the sink (delivery records only)


Correlation
Record ID, reference to the originating extraction, trace ID, timestamp, duration



Never recorded: cell values, sample rows, result bodies, driver error text,
credentials or connection configuration.
Where it is stored
Lineage records are append-only Avro files in the object store, partitioned
by UTC day. The object store seals every object it writes (see
Encryption at rest). LineageService.GetSourceActivity reads
this log. The FACE app does not show it today; it is an API call.

Warning: Scope of these controls

Timestamps are the server's clock.
Retention belongs to the log pipeline. FACE emits audit records to
standard output. How long they are kept, who can read them and how they are
protected once written are properties of the log pipeline your deployment
runs.
Hashing is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation. Anyone who already knows an
identifier can compute its hash and find that identifier's events.
A camera ingest records zero rows. A camera sends frames, not rows. The
record therefore calls the ingest an extraction with a row count of zero, and
carries no frame count.
A query fingerprint is not the query. It proves two reads had the same
shape. It cannot reconstruct the values that were used.

docs/architecture/security/network-egres.title: Network egress controls
docs/architecture/security/network-egres.body:
Network egress controls

Connectors dial addresses that a person typed into a form, from inside your
cluster. A fetcher with no address policy can be turned into a request-forgery
tool: pointed at the cloud metadata service, the cluster's internal services or
FACE itself. FACE's connectors therefore share one hardened dialer,
one connector network layer, and one address policy.
Encrypted connectors only
No connector may run without its security settings, and every connection moves
off plaintext. FACE offers no plaintext connector. One
connector security policy is applied in two halves:

What holds for every connector, judged from the connection record by the
shared store library: insecure_skip_verify is refused, a Postgres or
MySQL ssl_mode that allows cleartext is refused (use require, verify-ca
or verify-full), a Kafka security_protocol of plaintext or
sasl_plaintext is refused (use sasl_ssl), and a cleartext scheme on any
address setting, bootstrap server or extra property is refused.
What only the connector knows, checked by FACE: what an empty setting or
a bare host:port is dialled as, and which credential it signs in with.

Every write (creating a connection, or registering a partner connection
manifest) refuses a connection with problems. A stored connection that does
not meet the policy is refused on every read, and ListConnections reports
the verdict per row in plain words naming the setting to fix. Nothing deletes
or rewrites a stored connection.
The quickstart data sources Runink hosts are registered the same way: Postgres and
MySQL with ssl_mode = "require", and Kafka with security_protocol = "sasl_ssl" and
SCRAM-SHA-512, trusting the quickstart CA certificate.
The connector address policy
Every outbound connection a connector makes is checked against an egress policy
on the address actually dialled, after DNS resolution, on every dial. The policy
blocks internal addresses unless an operator explicitly allows a connection to
reach them, and it never dials the cloud instance-metadata service. An address
that cannot be checked is not dialled.
Allowing a connection to reach internal addresses
Some sources, such as a dock-door reader or a cold-room gateway, are internal by
nature. Whether a connection may reach internal addresses is set per connection
with the property allow_internal_network (true or false). The decision is
stored with the connection, not in an environment variable that would reopen
every fetch on the instance.
A refused internal address is reported in words an operator can act on, and the
message names the property to set if that address is genuinely the source you
mean.
Proxies, redirects and response size

No ambient proxy. Connector HTTP clients ignore environment-configured
proxies, so the policy always judges the real destination.
Redirects stay on the named host. Connector HTTP clients never follow a
redirect to a different host:
refusing to follow a redirect from … to …. This keeps a tenant's credential
from travelling to a host the connection never named.
Bounded timeouts and bodies. Every connector client has a whole-request
timeout, and bounded dial and TLS-handshake times. Response bodies are read up
to a cap. A body over the cap is refused outright, never reported as a short
but complete answer.

The Snowflake and Databricks drivers are handed the same transport through their
driver-level transport hooks, so the address policy applies to every address
those drivers dial.
Read-only SQL
Every executable SQL path goes through ValidateSQL. That covers the generic SQL
service, which also serves the agent loop's run_sql tool, and the Postgres,
MySQL, Snowflake and Databricks connectors. FACE runs read-only queries;
statements that could change data are refused. Warehouse connectors pass query
parameters as real bound parameters, never by string interpolation.
IPv6-first, IPv4 fully supported
FACE is deployed IPv6-first, while many warehouses and cloud APIs are reachable
only over IPv4. Both have to work, so:

No code pins an address family. Every dial uses Go's "tcp" network with
no negative FallbackDelay, which gives RFC 8305 Happy Eyeballs behaviour.
TestNothingPinsAnAddressFamily fails on any tcp4, tcp6, ip4 or ip6
literal, or on a negative fallback delay.
Host:port strings are built and parsed properly. Code uses
net.JoinHostPort to build addresses and net.SplitHostPort to parse them,
never string concatenation or a colon search. Those break every IPv6 literal.
TestNoHandBuiltHostPortInTheBackend parses the backend source and
fails on the old patterns. Mutation tests in the same file prove the guard can
fail.


Warning: Scope of these controls

Read-only is not authorisation. ValidateSQL keeps queries to reads. It
does not limit which tables a query reads. That limit is the database
account's own permissions, so connect FACE with a least-privilege, read-only
database user.
Parsing an address is not reaching it. Correct dialling code gives an
