IPv6-only pod no route to an IPv4-only provider. That route is NAT64 or egress
configuration in the deployment.

docs/architecture/security/compliance/.title: Compliance posture
docs/architecture/security/compliance/.body:
Compliance posture

What "SOC 2-oriented" means here
FACE's controls are designed around the concerns that SOC 2's trust services
criteria address: access control, confidentiality, change and configuration
integrity, and monitoring. The earlier pages in this section describe those
controls. Some rules and log fields in the code carry ISO 27001, ISO 42001,
ISO 31000 or SOC 2 tags. Those tags are labels a developer attached to a
control, used for classification and reporting. They are not the result of an
assessment.

Warning: No certification is claimed. Nothing in this documentation states or
implies that FACE, or any deployment of it, holds a SOC 2 report, ISO 27001 or
ISO 42001 certification, a FedRAMP authorisation or a CMMC certification, or is
suitable for ITAR-controlled data. If your procurement requires one of these,
ask Runink directly. This documentation is not evidence of any of them.

Compliance environment variables are declarations
FACE's compliance analysis reads four compliance environment variables and
reports their values. Each is an operator's assertion about the deployment,
reported as such:



Variable
What FACE does with it




ENFORCE_AUDIT_LOGGING
Reports it. It gates nothing: audit logging is always on regardless of its value.


REQUIRE_HITL
Reports it.


DATABASE_ENGINE
Reports it. It is not probed.


PRIMARY_SERVER_URL
Reports it. It is not probed.



FACE does not refuse to start when these variables are missing. In the analysis
prompt, each value is labelled OPERATOR DECLARATION with the variable named,
followed by a NOTE TO THE ASSESSOR explaining that a declaration is not evidence
the control exists. Where FACE can observe a fact directly, such as audit logging
being always on, it reports that fact separately as OBSERVED in code.
TestEnvironmentDerivedControlsAreLabelledAsDeclarationsNotFindings pins this labelling in both directions.
The controls that keep a human in the loop are the ones described in
AI safety: review of proposed actions, the
per-agent action allowlists, and agent email that is only ever drafted.
Evidence you can check
Many of the controls in this section are enforced by a named test. FACE is
proprietary; the tests are available to customers under NDA, and each name below is
what a reviewer passes to go test -run:



Control
Test




The unauthenticated surface is exactly the documented list
TestAuthExemptionsAreOnlyTheApprovedSet


An mTLS identity never replaces a session
TestAVerifiedMTLSPeerStillNeedsABearerToken


No insecure gRPC or TLS transport in any Go package
TestNoInsecureTransportInAnyPackage


No plaintext downgrade on runner dials
TestRunnerDialDoesNotDowngradeToAPlaintextRunner


A connection that allows cleartext is refused
TestConnectionSecurityProblemsJoinsBothHalves and TestConnectionNotSecured


Consensus is served only over mTLS
TestRaftServiceIsNeverOnTheApplicationListener


A revocation reaches runners
TestARevokeOnTheControlPlaneIsRefusedOnARunner


Lineage records carry no data values
TestNoResultValuesReachAnyLineageRecord


Local secret-bearing files are 0600/0700
TestPersistCometUsesRestrictiveModes and TestKnowledgeCorpusIsNotWorldReadable


No service token is ever invented
TestFaceNeverInventsAServiceToken


Guardrail docs match the code and can fire
TestEveryRuleDocDeclaresItsEnforcement, TestDocumentedRulesMatchGetJudge and the firing tests


Unmapped agents cannot reach the loop
TestUnmappedAgentIdCannotReachTheLoop


Voice refusals never reach the model, and transcripts are never logged
TestRefusedUtteranceNeverReachesTheModel


No address family is pinned
TestNothingPinsAnAddressFamily


Compliance env vars are labelled as declarations
TestEnvironmentDerivedControlsAreLabelledAsDeclarationsNotFindings



Many of these source-scanning guards carry a positive control or a
mutation test, which deliberately breaks the protected property and requires
the guard to fail by name. Without one, a guard could pass while checking
nothing.

Warning: Scope of this page

Oriented is not compliant. A control designed with SOC 2 in mind is not a
control an auditor has tested over a period of time.
Tests prove code behaviour, not operations. They say nothing about how a
deployment is operated: access reviews, change management, incident response,
log retention and key custody all belong to your organisation and to the
platform operator.
A compliance tag is a classification, not a finding. A rule tagged
ISO42001 is a rule someone associated with that standard. Nobody has assessed
it against the standard.

docs/user-guide/agents/.title: Model cards
docs/user-guide/agents/.body:
Agent model cards

A model card describes one of FACE's agents in plain language: what it is for, what
it reads, what it hands a person, who has to approve it, which model it runs on, and
where it stops. There is one card for each kind of work you meet in FACE. What an agent
finds shows on Ask, its options on Options, and what it drafts for approval on
Actionable Twins.
Several cards cover more than one agent, because those agents do one job together.
These cards are written for buyers, evaluators and operators. The mechanics behind
them are on the Analysis & evidence pages, which these cards link
to rather than repeat.
One rule for every card
FACE drafts. A person decides. Every claim, short-pay, filing, order, quarantine,
remediation and repair that an agent proposes is a recommendation for a named approver.
Nothing is sent, filed, paid or settled until someone with the authority approves it, and
the server records who did. The one exception is FACE's own operational
self-healing: restarting, isolating, rolling back or scaling FACE
itself runs automatically from a fixed list, and an operator can switch it off. The
approval tiers and the decision log are described in
Auditability & lineage
and Agents & oversight.
The cards



Card
What it helps with
Base model




Claims & recovery
Shortage, OS&D and SLA claims, filing windows and the letter for approval.
General


Freight invoice audit
Carrier invoices against the rate confirmation, SLA credits and spend.
General


Customs & trade documents
Customs holds, document cross-checks and draft trade documents.
General


Compliance review

General, plus code for code checks


Insurance claim files
Assembling the cargo claim file for an adjuster.
General


Cold chain & telemetry

Maintenance

Documents & plans (vision)

General

General

General

General


Counterparty background check

General


Customer analysis
Cost to serve, service performance, claims, payment behaviour and concentration per business account.
General



How to read a card
Every card has the same sections:

What it does: one sentence, then the jobs it handles.
What it reads: the records, documents and systems it takes in.
What it produces: what you get back, and in what form.
Human oversight: what a person approves, and what the agent can never do by itself.
Model: the base model it runs on.
Where it runs and data handling: where inference happens.
Guardrails: the policies it follows, in plain words.
How to read its results: what a result shows, what stays with a person, and
when it declines or says data is missing.

To see what each agent produces on real data, load the
quickstart estate and ask about it on Ask.
Facts shared by every card
Models. FACE sends each model call to one of three tiers on the deployment's model
plane, chosen by the kind of task (see
Sovereign models):

General reasoning: most agents.
Code: rule checks written as code.
Vision: documents and images; it starts on demand.

Each tier serves the deployment's own models.
Many of the figures on these cards cite the records they came from. See
Evidence documents.
Where inference runs. Every agent calls the model plane of its own FACE
deployment: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, the customer's own cloud on
Cloud and their own servers on On-premises. FACE calls no outside AI service on any plan. Records an agent reads are passed to the model as fenced,
untrusted data, never as instructions (see AI safety).
The connections you configure still reach their own systems, and an approved action,
such as an email sent through a connected account, goes where that action says.
Guardrails. Each agent's requests are checked against its guardrail rules
before a prompt reaches the model, and Every proposed action is independently reviewed before a person decides.
Both are described in Agents & oversight and
AI safety, including the scope of each.

docs/user-guide/agents/claims-recovery/.title: Claims & recovery
docs/user-guide/agents/claims-recovery/.body:
Claims & recovery

Agent: the claims agent (claims in ExecuteLoop), with the claims and
recovery evidence documents.
What it does
It puts a freight claim together from your own shipping records and drafts the
paperwork for a person to approve. Its jobs:

Shortage at delivery. Compares the manifest weight with the weighbridge reading
and the counts received, and works out what is short and what it is worth.
Over, short and damaged receipts. Compares the purchase order, the bill of
lading and the receiving count, and prepares the OS&D report.
Filing windows. Works out the notice and suit dates from the delivery date and
the named regime, and orders open claims by the earliest deadline.
Disputes and recovery. Prepares the notice of intent to claim, the statement of
position and the subrogation demand.
Recovery procedures. Ranks the recovery work with the most money at stake first,
for example SLA breach refunds, accessorial and duplicate-charge disputes, and
return patterns worth a closer look.

What it reads
Manifests, bills of lading, purchase orders, goods-received records, weighbridge
events, carrier tracking milestones, SLA records, invoices and the business rules
that Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only
queries against the connection a run was started with. Other agents can hand it a
sub-task with delegate_to_claims.
What it produces

Evidence documents from the closed vocabulary: OSD_REPORT,
NOTICE_OF_INTENT_TO_CLAIM, STATEMENT_OF_POSITION and SUBROGATION_DEMAND. Each
figure cites the record it came from, and each deadline names the rule that set it.
See Evidence documents.
Action cards on Actionable Twins (claims play), each with one proposed next step, such as "send
this claim letter to the carrier".
A short recovery plan: two or three procedures, ranked by money recovered, each tied
to the records behind it.

Human oversight

A claims handler approves every claim letter, dispute and demand before it reaches
a carrier. Approval seals the evidence document; rejection needs a reason.
The agent never files a claim, contacts a carrier or withholds a payment on its own.
A computed deadline is an input for the person deciding, not legal advice.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. Your records reach the model as fenced,
untrusted data. See Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Never invents a figure. A missing rate or document is named as missing, and no
amount is given in its place.
Does not decide or score claims on the basis of a claimant's name, demographics or
location, and does not lowball settlements for particular areas.
Does not fabricate weather events or disruptions to build a force majeure defence.
Does not build defamatory profiles of carriers, and does not scrape partner portals
or private systems without authorisation.
Stays on claims and recovery work; warehouse routing and macro forecasting belong to
other agents.

How to read its results

It works from your records. Rates come from your contract file, and a rate that
isn't in it is reported as not stated.
It doesn't establish liability. A claim document assembles the file; the carrier,
an adjuster or a court decides.
A pattern that looks like return abuse is a lead for a person to check, not a
finding of fraud.
When a source could not be read, the document records the figure as absent with a
reason, such as NO_BACKING_RECORD or NOT_STATED_ON_DOCUMENT.

docs/user-guide/agents/freight-invoice-a.title: Freight invoice audit
docs/user-guide/agents/freight-invoice-a.body:
Freight invoice audit

Agent: the finance agent (finance in ExecuteLoop), with the rate-confirmation
and SLA evidence documents.
What it does
It checks what carriers bill against what you agreed, and drafts the short-pay or
credit request for finance to approve. Its jobs:

Invoice against rate confirmation. Finds accessorial lines that the rate
confirmation doesn't authorise, units billed inside free time, and rates above the
one agreed.
SLA credits. Works out the service credits owed under an SLA clause for late
pickups or missed delivery windows.
Order, invoice and bill of lading. Finds where the three disagree on quantity,
and by how much.
Spend oversight. Sorts transactions into categories with a stated confidence,
flags spend that departs from its baseline, and compares options by cost-benefit,
total cost of ownership and cost to serve.

What it reads
Carrier invoices, signed rate confirmations, master service agreements and their SLA
clauses, purchase orders, goods-received records, invoice lines, the general-ledger
chart you use, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data.
It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
What it produces

Evidence documents RATE_CON_ACCESSORIAL_AUDIT (accessorials billed above the rate
confirmation) and MSA_SLA_COMPLIANCE_AUDIT (service credits owed). Their headline
amounts count as money only as described on
Action cards & money.
Action cards proposing a short-pay, a dispute or a credit request, on
Actionable Twins under the claims play.
For spend oversight: categorised transactions with a confidence, anomalies with the
observed and expected values side by side, and recommended actions.

Human oversight

An accounts-payable or finance lead approves every short-pay, dispute and credit
request. The agent never pays, withholds or credits money itself.
Budget reallocations and procurement changes it suggests are recommendations only.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Compares your invoice with your own rate confirmation, line by line. A rate the
confirmation doesn't state is reported as not stated, not disputed on a guess.
Refuses to falsify cost-benefit, total-cost-of-ownership or cost-to-serve results.
Refuses to fabricate or hide procurement spend to favour a vendor, and refuses to
invent market-rate benchmarks.
Stays on finance: claims disputes, dispatch, maintenance schedules and compliance
audits belong to other agents.

How to read its results

Its reference is your contract: every figure is measured against your own rate
confirmation.
Identified money is not recovered money. Only what a carrier credits or pays back
is recovered.
A transaction category comes with the agent's confidence. It is a suggestion for
your chart of accounts, not a posting.
When the contract, the invoice line or the SLA clause is missing, the figure is
reported as missing and no amount is given.

docs/user-guide/agents/customs-trade-doc.title: Customs & trade documents
docs/user-guide/agents/customs-trade-doc.body:
Customs & trade documents

Agent: the documentation agent (documentation in ExecuteLoop), with the
customs cards and the CUSTOMS_MANIFEST_EXCEPTION evidence document.
What it does
It reads your shipping and customs records, finds what is holding a shipment up or
doesn't match, and drafts the next document or step for your trade team. Its jobs:

Customs holds. Finds entries that are held, which release documents are still
missing, and the charges that have built up so far.
Document cross-checks. Compares the bill of lading, commercial invoice and
packing list for one shipment, and names where they disagree.
Weight against manifest. When the weighbridge and the manifest differ by more
than 5 %, drafts a manifest amendment.
Draft trade documents. When an order is ready for dispatch, drafts the bill of
lading, commercial invoice, packing list and customs declaration from your ERP
records, with the HS classification and Incoterm for review.

What it reads
Customs entry records, manifests, bills of lading, commercial invoices, packing lists,
weighbridge events, ERP order and shipping records, regulatory tables you provide, and
the rules Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only
queries against the connection a run was started with.
What it produces

Customs cards with a priority and a proposed next action, such as "request the
certificate of origin from the supplier". A customs manifest exception waits on
Actionable Twins under the disruptions play.
The CUSTOMS_MANIFEST_EXCEPTION evidence document, with each figure cited. See
Evidence documents.
Draft document payloads (bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list, customs
declaration), an HS classification and the Incoterm, for a person to check.

Human oversight

The customs or trade lead approves every next step and every document before it is
sent or filed.
The agent never files a declaration, submits a document to an authority or
amends a manifest on its own.
HS classifications are proposals. The declarant remains responsible for them.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Refuses to falsify or fabricate HS codes, commercial invoices, packing lists or
Incoterms to avoid a tariff or a check.
Never invents a figure. A document or value that isn't on file is named as missing.
Duty is kept out of avoidable port charges, so a delay's cost isn't inflated.

How to read its results

It gives no legal or customs advice. A computed date or limit is an input for the
person deciding.
A draft document is only as complete as the ERP record behind it. Missing fields
stay empty and are named, never filled with a plausible value.
It doesn't establish who caused a hold. It reports what the entry record says.

docs/user-guide/agents/compliance-review.title: Compliance review
docs/user-guide/agents/compliance-review.body:
Compliance review

Agents: the compliance agent (compliance) and Rules Recon (rules_recon).
What it does
It puts what your policies say next to what your systems actually do, names where they
part, and writes the next step in business language for the person who owns the
control. Its jobs:

Rules Recon. Finds the business and governance rules in your data, documents,
telemetry limits and code, and classifies each one:
Aligned: the implementation matches the policy.
Drift: both exist, but the implementation has moved away from the policy.
Shadow: logic runs in the data or code with no policy behind it.
Missing: a policy exists and nothing implements it.


Framework checks. Gives an overall status of Pass, Fail or Warning against the
frameworks you work to, and lists each violation with its rule and a remediation.
Personal data. Flags personal data shown without masking in reports, query results and logs,
and drafts the masking proposal and the data protection officer's notice.
Emissions and supplier risk. Works out freight emissions with the method beside
the figure, and summarises supplier compliance risk from the evidence provided.

What it reads
Policies, SOPs, contracts and SLAs; the running configuration and data of connected
systems; logs and report extracts; telemetry limits; and, for Rules Recon's code
checks, source code and configuration files. It can run read-only queries against the
connection a run was started with.
What it produces

A list of rules, each with its plain-English logic, the source it came from, its
severity, its maturity (Low, Medium or High) and its reconciliation status. You see
them on Why, where each rule's policy drawer sets its enforcement posture.
A compliance status, violations with a remediation each, and an audit trail of which
systems were checked and with what result, on the Compliance view opened from
Actionable Twins. See
Compliance, finance, operations.
Remediation orders for a person to assign, route and decide, listed in the
Waiting for you lane on Actionable Twins and on the Compliance view.

Human oversight

A person assigns, routes and decides every remediation order, and the server records
who did each (AssignRemediation, SetRemediationRoute, DecideRemediation).
Rule enforcement posture is set by an operator (UpdateRulePolicy). The agent can't
change a finding's status that way.
The agent never changes configuration, masking or data. Its remediations are steps
for a person to take, such as a ticket or an escalation, never SQL or code fixes.

Model

Compliance and rule extraction: the general reasoning tier.
Rules Recon code checks: the code tier.

Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Cites the source of every rule, and doesn't invent files or policies. When nothing
is found, it reports no rules.
Reports no confidence score for its own verdict. The reconciliation status is the
verdict.
Refuses to create rules that discriminate, that retaliate against a particular
employee, supplier or partner, or that bypass audits, governance checks or ethical
sourcing obligations.
Refuses to falsify emission figures or supplier ESG ratings, to weaken business
continuity plans, or to bypass the personal-data masking and breach-notice triggers.

How to read its results

It doesn't certify compliance with any framework. A Pass is the agent's reading of
the evidence it was given.
"Not assessed" is a separate result from "passed". Where evidence is absent, the
control is not shown as green.
A breach-notice draft is a starting point for the data protection officer, not a
legal determination.
It gives no legal advice.

docs/user-guide/agents/insurance-claim-f.title: Insurance claim files
docs/user-guide/agents/insurance-claim-f.body:
Insurance claim files

What it is: FACE's cargo insurance evidence documents, and the general model when
you ask questions about a file.
What it does
It assembles the cargo claim file for an adjuster, so the adjuster starts from the
records rather than from a search. It never decides cover. Its jobs:

First notice of loss. Builds the FNOL document from the loss records, and
names what hasn't been stated.
Cargo loss survey. Sets out what was lost or damaged, and its value, from the
records.
Warranty compliance audit. Checks the shipment's records against the warranty
conditions the policy states, such as a temperature band.
Recovery. Prepares the subrogation demand against the carrier.

What it reads
The policy records you hold (wording, warranties, declared value, deductible),
certificates, loss reports, temperature and custody records, carrier contracts and the
claim's own documents.
What it produces
Evidence documents FNOL, CARGO_LOSS_SURVEY, WARRANTY_COMPLIANCE_AUDIT and
SUBROGATION_DEMAND, each attached to an action card with one proposed next step. The
cards wait on Actionable Twins; the FNOL, survey and subrogation cards sit under
the claims play.
Every fact cites the record it came from, and a missing figure is recorded as absent
with a reason. See Evidence documents.
Human oversight

The adjuster, or another person with authority, decides. The agent never
underwrites, prices a risk, accepts or declines cover, sets a reserve or settles a
claim.
No finding code says VOID, DECLINED, REPUDIATED or anything like it. Those are
an underwriter's words.
Approving a card seals its document and records who approved it.

Model
Questions you ask about a file in free text go to the general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails
The documents are built to these policies:

Never invents a warranty condition the policy doesn't state, for example a
temperature band inferred from the word "reefer".
Never reads a missing declared value as zero, and never substitutes an invoiced
value for an undeclared one.
Never states that something caused a loss unless the records say so. A temperature
reading and a crushed carton are two facts, not a cause and an effect.
Never leaves out a loss figure the records state, and never discourages a claim.
Never treats protected characteristics, or postcode and nationality as proxies for
them, as grounds for anything.

How to read its results

A document is a file, not a decision. It doesn't establish that a loss is or isn't
covered.
It works from the records you hold.
FACE's approval tiers govern who may approve an action inside FACE; a claim
handler's delegated authority stays with your own process (see
Auditability & lineage).
A free-text answer from the general model is the model's reading of the file, not a
document. Check it against the cited records.

docs/user-guide/agents/cold-chain-teleme.title: Cold chain & telemetry
docs/user-guide/agents/cold-chain-teleme.body:
Cold chain & telemetry

Agent: the telemetry agent (telemetry in ExecuteLoop), with the
TEMPERATURE_EXCURSION and CHAIN_OF_CUSTODY_AUDIT evidence documents.
What it does
It reads sensor and telematics data, works out whether a load really left its stated
band and for how long, and drafts the quarantine, probe or reroute for a quality
manager to approve. Its jobs:

Temperature excursions. Measures time out of the stated band, gaps in the log,
and the load's exposure when the records state its value.
Sensor or product. Tells a stuck or silent sensor apart from a real change in
temperature.
Site thresholds. Flags speeding, perishable dwell at the dock and weighbridge
differences against the thresholds your site states.
Fleet and yard safety. Ranks events with a safety impact first, such as a
hazardous-goods segregation problem or a driver in distress.
Custody gaps. Finds intervals longer than the stated check-in cadence, door
events with no task, and loads with no events at all.

What it reads
Temperature and humidity readings, reefer logs, GPS, speed, fuel and engine data,
weighbridge events, custody events, dispatch states and the thresholds your records
state. Telemetry arrives through the connections described in
Telemetry. It can run read-only queries against the
connection a run was started with.
What it produces

Excursion and custody evidence documents, each figure cited. See
Evidence documents.
Action cards with a priority and one proposed step, such as "hold the load and
probe the core before release". They wait on Actionable Twins under the cold
chain play, and each reefer with readings out of band is pinned on its Map view.
On Options, the what-if options for a cold-chain decision, each scored on the
share of temperature readings past a limit their own row states. See
Action cards & money.
Safety notices for a supervisor, ranked by urgency.

Human oversight

A quality manager or supervisor approves every quarantine, reroute and release.
The agent never adjusts a reefer controller, locks or unlocks a crane, stops a
conveyor or reroutes a vehicle itself. It can propose a step or raise a cue as a
request; a person acts.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

No stated band, no breach. FACE never assumes a threshold the source didn't
provide, and never borrows an industry norm.
A missing reading is "not measured", never zero. A gap in the log is reported as a
gap.
Refuses to alter, suppress or fabricate sensor, GPS, speed, fuel or driver records.
Refuses to bypass hazardous-goods segregation rules or crane safety locks.
Refuses to run equipment control commands without a person's authorisation.
Stays on monitoring, cold chain, fleet telematics and yard safety.

How to read its results

A surface or air reading isn't the product's core temperature. The card says to
probe the core; it doesn't certify the product.
Exposure is stated only when the records give the load value with a currency.
Otherwise it is absent as "not measured".
Any projection of when a load will leave its band is labelled as modelled, not
measured.
An unrecorded handoff is not a break in custody. Custody findings are statements
about the record, never about the goods or the people.

docs/user-guide/agents/maintenance/.title: Maintenance
docs/user-guide/agents/maintenance/.body:
Maintenance

Agent: the predictive maintenance agent (predictive_maintenance in
ExecuteLoop), with the EQUIPMENT_LIMIT_APPROACH evidence document and the
AnalyzeTelemetry API call. Its cards wait on Actionable Twins under the
maintenance play.
What it does
It reads equipment sensor logs, says how far each asset is from the limit its feed
states and in which order to act, and drafts the intervention for a maintenance
planner. Its jobs:

Trend to a stated limit. Reports the margin left and, when the readings move
steadily towards the limit, when a straight line through the first and last readings
would reach it.
Prioritise. Orders the work by safety first, then by the impact on dependent
lines and shipments.
Plan the work. Drafts the work order, a maintenance window in the nearest planned
downtime, and a spare-parts request when stock is below the reorder point your
inventory feed states.

What it reads
Equipment readings such as vibration, bearing and oil temperature, pressure and
battery state; the limits the feed or maker states; maintenance logs; production
schedules; and spare-part stock levels. It can run read-only queries against the
connection a run was started with.
What it produces

The EQUIPMENT_LIMIT_APPROACH evidence document, with the readings it used, so a
technician can redo the sum. See
Evidence documents.
Action cards with a priority and a proposed intervention.
Draft work orders and parts requests.

Human oversight

A maintenance planner or supervisor approves every repair, shutdown, parts order
and schedule change.
The agent never shuts equipment down, overrides an alarm or orders parts itself.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Uses only the limit your feed or the maker states. It never substitutes an industry
norm or another asset's limit.
Refuses to override safety shutdowns, alarms or hazardous-materials procedures.
Refuses to alter or delete maintenance and compliance records, or sensor and
telematics data.
Doesn't neglect the safety needs of particular sites or regions when it ranks work.

How to read its results

A trend is not a forecast. It gives no failure probability, confidence score or
remaining useful life. A straight line through two readings supports none of them.
With no stated limit, or too few readings, it writes no limit card and says why.
When readings wander instead of trending, it says the crossing can't be projected.

docs/user-guide/agents/stock-and-demand/.title: Stock & demand
docs/user-guide/agents/stock-and-demand/.body:
Stock & demand

Agent: the fulfilment agent (fulfilment in ExecuteLoop), working with FACE's
statistics engine.
What it does
It reads stock, demand and lead times, says per item whether to do nothing, order now
or expedite, and drafts the order for a buyer to approve. Its jobs:

Reorder decisions. Works out days of cover and states which of your reorder
bounds was crossed, and by how much.
Forecasts. Reads the statistics engine's forecast, names the method that was
used and how much history it had, and adjusts safety stock from it.
Purchase orders. Drafts the order, with an expedite quantity and its premium
freight cost kept separate from normal replenishment.
Sourcing and service. Compares suppliers and carriers on the records you hold,
measures on-time-in-full, and finds lanes worth consolidating.
Dispatch documents. When an order is ready for dispatch, drafts the shipping
documents (see Customs & trade documents).

What it reads
Stock on hand and on order, demand history, lead times, reorder points and bounds,
supplier and carrier records, order and delivery records, and the rules
Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only queries
against the connection a run was started with.
What it produces

Action cards proposing a purchase order, an expedite or no action, each with the
figures behind it, on Actionable Twins under the inventory play.
Operational procedures, ranked by the money and time they save.

Human oversight

A buyer approves every purchase order and expedite. The agent never places an order
with a supplier on its own.
Dispatch priorities and allocations it proposes are recommendations only.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Forecasts come from FACE's statistics engine, not from a language model. See
Statistics & ML.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Uses the reorder points and bounds you set. It never invents them.
Refuses to force an order through or bypass a budget.
Doesn't favour suppliers on demographics, and doesn't starve particular regions or
groups of stock during a shortage.
Refuses to reorder dispatch to favour anyone over your SLA commitments.
Refuses to ignore temperature excursions or suppress cold-chain alerts to save cost
or time.

How to read its results

A forecast is not "exact stock needs". It comes with its method and the history it
had, so you can judge how far to trust it.
With too little history, the statistics engine declines to forecast rather than
guessing.

docs/user-guide/agents/returns/.title: Returns
docs/user-guide/agents/returns/.body:
Returns

Agent: the reverse logistics agent (reverse_logistics in ExecuteLoop), with
dock triage (TriageReturnItem) and the RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence document.
What it does
It checks each return against the contract window and the authorisation, applies your
disposition policy the same way every time, and drafts the call for the returns
supervisor. Its jobs:

Window and quantities. Finds returns received after the contract window, units
short of or over the authorisation, damaged units, and the value at stake.
Disposition. Grades a returned item at the dock and proposes restock,
refurbish, liquidate or recycle.
Warranty and recovery. Checks warranty periods against the records you hold,
and compares repair cost with expected recovery.
Routing. Proposes where a return should go and which returns to collect
together.
Hand-off. Passes a claims question to the claims agent.

What it reads
Return authorisations, original delivery records, contract return windows, grading
results and repair estimates, warranty records, and the capabilities of your returns
facilities. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started
with.
What it produces

Dock triage results: the grade and the disposition it maps to. Recovery yield,
refurbishment cost and a routing destination are not derived, because FACE holds no
pricing, cost or facility data for returns, and every response says so. See
Simulation & twins.
The RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence document, with cited figures.
Action cards with a proposed response to the customer or a routing step, on
Actionable Twins under the fulfilment play.

Human oversight

The returns supervisor makes the disposition call and approves any response to the
customer.
Triage moves no stock and raises no credit or refund.

Model
The general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Follows your written disposition policy. The answer for a grade doesn't depend on
who is on the dock.
A grade it doesn't recognise is refused, never guessed.
Uses your own grading and repair figures. It looks up no secondary-market prices.
Doesn't grade returns differently because of who the customer is.
Refuses to inflate refurbishment grades or to record a disposal as recycling.
Refuses to route hazardous or electronic waste improperly, or to skip e-waste
certification.

How to read its results

It doesn't issue refunds or credits, or move stock.
A pattern of returns that looks unusual is a lead for a person to check, not a
finding of abuse.
It doesn't certify disposal of hazardous or electronic waste.

docs/user-guide/agents/yard-and-transpor.title: Yard & transport
docs/user-guide/agents/yard-and-transpor.body:
Yard & transport

Agents: the twins orchestrator (twins), the route twin (route_twin) and the
common operational picture (cop), with the yard, border, custody and disruption
cards.
What it does
It reads yard snapshots, border and port events and transport records, flags the
trailer, crossing or container that is costing money now, and drafts the action for
the supervisor. Its jobs:

Yard capacity. Finds when the yard is over capacity and which arrivals were
never recorded.
Border waits. Works out detention from dwell time and the stated cost per hour,
and proposes "transmit corrected documents" when the recorded cause is a document
problem.
Demurrage and detention. Separates days caused by documents from days caused by
congestion.
Service disruption. Records a disruption and its effect on open orders.
Routes. Ranks the routes your routing provider returns on the criteria you name,
with emissions per mode where a factor is stated.
One picture. Ranks events from several sources by priority, life safety first,
and flags events seen by only one source.
Orchestration. The twins orchestrator maps each event to the right action card
and hands work to the other agents on these cards.

What it reads
Yard snapshots and appointments, border crossing and port events, container free time
and gate events, custody events, carrier and lane records, routes from your routing
provider, sensor and camera findings, and the twin graph.
It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
What it produces

Action cards on Actionable Twins, each with a priority and one proposed action. Route
proposals also show on its Map view. See
Action cards & money.
Evidence documents such as CHAIN_OF_CUSTODY_AUDIT and SERVICE_DISRUPTION.
A ranked list of routes and carriers, and a prioritised list of current events.

Human oversight

A supervisor approves every action on a card, through TwinsService.ExecuteAction.
Rejection needs a reason.
The agents never dispatch a vehicle, book a carrier or send anything to a transport
system on their own.
Every proposed action is independently reviewed before a person decides.
The reviewer's verdict is shown on the card. See
Agents & oversight.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Distances and travel times come from your routing provider.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Never makes up a distance or a time. A route the provider couldn't compute is
"unavailable", never zero.
A missing cause, capacity or cost figure is reported as missing.
Doesn't deprioritise neighbourhoods or regions on socioeconomic or demographic
grounds, and doesn't recommend hoarding capacity or price gouging.
Refuses to de-anonymise people from aggregate trends, and refuses to fabricate
sustainability figures.

How to read its results

An unrecorded handoff is not a break in custody.
A ranked route is only as good as the provider's answer and the criteria you named.
An event flagged as single-source hasn't been confirmed by a second source.
It doesn't establish who caused a delay beyond what the records state.

docs/user-guide/agents/options-and-appro.title: Options & approvals
docs/user-guide/agents/options-and-appro.body:
Options & approvals

What it is: what you use on Simulate › Options to see what you could do about a
run's findings and what each option is worth, and FACE's decision-authority policy,
which decides who must approve each action on Actionable Twins.
What it does
It lays out the choices before anyone commits money, and makes sure the decision to act
is taken by the right number of named people. Its jobs:

Options. For the decision behind the selected run's checks, it scores each
option on one shared measure with a 95% range. It marks one Recommended only when
that option's range clears the next one's and the figure as measured. Otherwise it
says No clear winner on this data, and why.
Scenarios. It generates scenarios from your estate's domains, links and rules,
and tests them against your data. Options lists them under "What FACE tested", with
a Graph view and a New Simulation action.
Cost and benefit. When you state the costs and benefits of a change, the
scenario agent is asked to work out net present value (at 8 % when no discount rate
is given) and payback, and to flag payback above 36 months as high risk.
Approval tier. For each proposed action, the policy names the tier: advisory,
one named approver, two different named approvers, automatic, or denied.

What it reads
The selected run's checks and the figures it measured, your estate's domains and
rules, the scenario parameters you set in New Simulation, time series and
operational records, and the output of the statistics engine. The approval policy
reads an action's type, value and safety or regulatory flags.
What it produces

Option cards on Options. Each shows the lever and the change, what it was
measured to do over the run's rows with its range, and whether it was recommended.
An option the data cannot score is Not measured, with the data it needs, and is
never ranked.
Scenario results on Options: what each scenario tested and how it ended. The
status counts, what went to the twins and the run step by step are in the folded
How FACE knows this. See Simulate and
Simulation & twins.
A card on Actionable Twins when you press Send for approval. It lands in
Waiting for you and shows the person approving it what they are approving. See
Action cards & money.
For each card, its approval tier and the rule that set it.

Human oversight

Options executes nothing and changes nothing in your systems. Sending an option for
approval is a separate act by a person, and approving it records the decision; it
runs nothing by itself.
An option sent for approval is never automatic. It needs one named person, or two
different named people, as the policy answers it.
Safety and regulatory actions always need a person, and a dual approval needs two
different people.
Every decision is recorded on the decision log. See
Auditability & lineage.

Model

Comparing options is computed from the rows the run stored.
Scenarios and their explanation: the general reasoning tier.
Causal and Bayesian analysis runs in the statistics engine, not in the language
model. See Statistics & ML.

Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Comparing options reads only what the run stored. It never re-reads a source.
Every scenario figure is worked out from the assumptions you state. When a discount
rate isn't stated, the default is shown.
Refuses scenarios that assume one demographic group is superior to another, or that
attribute failures to protected groups.
Refuses scenarios aimed at price fixing, predatory or discriminatory pricing, market
cornering or sabotage.
Refuses to skew forecasts to influence orders or budgets, or to hide anomalies.
Stays on analysis: booking freight or writing rules belong elsewhere.

How to read its results

An option's figure covers the rows the run read. A fetch reads a bounded sample
of each table, and the card says so when it did.
Read whether an effect was estimated or assumed. A lead-time option's effect is
estimated from the shipments that took it. A temperature option's effect is an assumption, and the card says it is not estimated.
"No clear winner" is an answer. It means the ranges overlap on this data, not
that FACE failed.
A scenario result is your own assumptions written out formally. It isn't a
prediction of what will happen. The scenarios in a run cover only what was
simulated: read the counts before treating the results as covering the whole
estate.
The approval tier says who must approve. A recorded approval shows who approved,
not how carefully they reviewed.

docs/user-guide/agents/field-readings/.title: Field readings (edge)
docs/user-guide/agents/field-readings/.body:
Field readings (edge)

What it is: the field-reading narrative, which writes up a walk with a handheld
reader such as the Flipper edge reader.
What it does
It turns what a handheld reader picked up on a site walk into one plain paragraph that
says what was found and, just as clearly, what the walk does not establish. Its jobs:

Phrase the walk. Writes one paragraph over the walk's readings.
Keep the distinctions. Keeps apart readings that support the walk's claim and ambient readings taken at the same time.
Say what it doesn't prove. Includes the walk's "what this does not establish"
sentence every time.

What it reads
The readings of one walk as the reader's connector reported them, such as NFC,
125 kHz RFID, infrared, sub-GHz, 1-Wire and Wi-Fi sightings, with each reading's role
and quality, and the walk's own statement of what it doesn't establish.
What it produces
One short paragraph, with no headings, bullets, recommendations or next steps. When the
paragraph can't be written from the input alone, it says exactly what is missing
instead.
Human oversight

The paragraph is a report. It proposes no action. Any action on a site walk is a
person's decision.
It changes no figure.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
The narrative records which model wrote it.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. Labels from a field reader are treated as
untrusted, because anyone nearby can influence what a radio reader hears. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Never changes a figure.
An enclosure or device temperature measures the equipment, never the cargo, and the
paragraph keeps that qualifier.

How to read its results

A sighting says a thing was heard. It isn't a location, a count or an inventory.
Radio occupancy says a band was busy, not what was transmitting.
It doesn't identify people or say whether anyone was authorised to be there.

docs/user-guide/agents/data-posture/.title: Data posture
docs/user-guide/agents/data-posture/.body:
Data posture

Agent: the posture agent (ai_posture), behind PostureService.
What it does
It reads your connected tables and documents, groups them into business domains, and
describes what each domain's data is missing.
Its jobs:

Map the estate. Groups tables that share keys, entities or subject into domains,
and names how each domain relates to the others, including links of business meaning
where no key is shared.
Describe each domain. Its reading of a domain is shown as the model's. Grades,
readiness percentages and ratings it writes are not shown: only what the profiler
measures is (see Posture & maturity).
Name the incidents. Writes up material data-maturity incidents with severity,
impact, root cause, blast radius and a recommended fix.

What it reads
Table schemas, sample rows and extracted documents from the connections you
configure. Exploring a source never samples customer rows; reading rows is a separate,
bounded call (see Data sources).
What it produces
A posture snapshot: domains, their relationships, a maturity scorecard and incidents,
shown on Why. Results the agent wrote are marked as model-generated. See
Posture & maturity.
Human oversight

The data owner decides on every recommendation.
The agent never changes schemas, masking or access.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
Posture & maturity says which result came from where.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Builds the domain map from your schemas and samples. It doesn't invent tables or
domains.
Refuses to inflate readiness scores or data-quality grades without evidence.
Refuses to suggest or test dangerously open security settings, or to alter audit
logs.
Doesn't penalise vendors or regions on assumptions rather than measured evidence.
Stays on posture: fulfilment and claims belong to other agents.

How to read its results

A grade reflects the structure of the data it could read, not how the data is used.
A failed scan is an error, not a grade of F. A domain that couldn't be read is not
assessed, which is different from a pass.
Business-meaning links between domains are the model's inference. Check them before
relying on them.

docs/user-guide/agents/voice-dispatch/.title: Voice dispatch
docs/user-guide/agents/voice-dispatch/.body:
Voice dispatch

Agent: the voice dispatcher (voice), behind the phone line and the
calling screen. The FACE app's navigation has no calling page
today: the calling screen is not one of its routes.
What it does
It lets a driver ask out loud where the next stop is, what the customer asked for or
which door to use, and hear a short answer, with the call written to the log. Its jobs:

Answer the driver. Replies in a few spoken sentences from the dispatch record.
Log what was said. Picks out the events a driver reports, such as speeding, a
tyre-pressure warning, a long idle or an engine vibration, and writes them to the log.
Alert a person. Raises anything urgent, such as a driver in distress, to a
dispatcher.

What it reads
The transcript of what the driver said, the vehicle's position, the stop list and
customer notes on the dispatch record, and the rules
Rules Recon found in your data. Its only tool is a read-only
query.
What it produces

A short spoken reply, synthesised as speech.
Safety notifications and routing updates for a dispatcher.
The telematics events the driver reported, for a dispatcher. The call itself is
logged turn by turn.

Human oversight

A dispatcher acts on every alert and every routing change.
A call never changes routes or stops in your transport system.

Model

Reasoning: the general reasoning tier.
Speech recognition and speech synthesis run on services inside the deployment.

Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. A phone call is carried by your telephony
provider, which carries the audio. On a call, the audio is transcribed as it
arrives and then discarded, and the transcript is kept with the session. A caller's
words are never written to the process log.
Guardrails

The phone line is the one path a person can reach without an account, so every
utterance is screened before any model is called. A refusal is spoken to the caller. See
AI safety.
Distances are labelled as straight-line estimates.

How to read its results

For a driver in distress it alerts a person. It gives no legal or medical advice.
A transcript can mishear. Events it logs from speech are what the driver said, not
vehicle telemetry.

docs/user-guide/agents/documents-and-pla.title: Documents & plans (vision)
docs/user-guide/agents/documents-and-pla.body:
Documents & plans (vision)

What it is: FACE's image work: grading camera frames
(Vision & CCTV), the vision agent (vision), reading
photographed or scanned forms, and proposing elements from a picture of a site plan.

Note: Runs on the Server's vision model, which starts on demand. The first image request
after a quiet period takes longer while the model loads.

What it does
It reads images and turns them into fields, grades and
proposed elements that FACE and a person can check. Its jobs:

Camera frames. Grades the inspectable object in a frame: what it is, its
material, a damage grade (PRISTINE, DAMAGED, DEFECTIVE or DESTROYED) and an
estimated damage percentage. Optional detection draws one box per object of the
graded class.
Forms. Reads a photographed or scanned document, such as a bill of lading,
packing list or delivery note, when text extraction alone can't.
Site plans. Proposes zones, docks and yard slots from a picture of a plan, for an
operator to confirm.

What it reads
Frames pushed to FACE or sampled from RTSP/HTTP camera feeds, document images, and
plan images. Frames are downscaled before the model sees them.
What it produces

A graded frame with per-object results, each box labelled with the stage that drew
it, and notes that explain any absence. See Vision & CCTV.
Values read from a document image, each recorded with the outcome of the read
(READ, NOT_PRESENT_ON_DOCUMENT, ILLEGIBLE or EXTRACTION_FAILED). You attach a
document with the clip or camera on Ask, and Why shows what was attached to
the run. See
Evidence documents.
Proposed plan elements, which stay proposals until an operator confirms them, in the
Site plans panel on Actionable Twins › Map. See
Twin ontology & graph.

Human oversight

Nothing a vision model proposes from a plan is written to the twin graph until an
operator confirms it. See
Twin ontology & graph.
A grade is input for a person. It never approves, rejects or releases anything.
Any action taken on what a frame or a form shows goes through the same action-card
approval as everything else.

Model
The deployment's vision tier, started on demand.
The live camera view shows boxes only and grades nothing.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane. No outside AI service is called on any plan. See
Sovereign models.
Guardrails

A person is not a subject. People never appear in the graded objects, and a frame
with no inspectable object gets no grade rather than a low one.
Refuses to downgrade, hide or fake a camera assessment.
Refuses to steer a sensor cue into unlocking a crane, blinding a camera or standing
down a safety interlock, and refuses to plant false events into the shared
operational picture.
A model's confidence in a value it read from a document is recorded, never used as a
truth threshold.

How to read its results

A grade and a damage percentage are the vision model's estimate from downscaled
pixels. They aren't a physical inspection.
A retained evidence frame shows the reviewer what was assessed. It isn't a forensic
record.
It identifies no one.

docs/user-guide/agents/claims-leakage/.title: Claims leakage
docs/user-guide/agents/claims-leakage/.body:
Claims leakage

Agent: the claims leakage agent (claims_leakage in ExecuteLoop), with the
CLAIMS_LEAKAGE evidence document and the ReviewClaimsLeakage call.
What it does
It finds money your own records show is recoverable and has not been recovered, puts
the most urgent first, and drafts the next step for the person who approves the
recovery. Its jobs:

Losses never claimed. A shortage or damage on the receiving record with no claim
and no dispute file for the shipment.
Claims not served. A claim on file where the correspondence shows no written
notice sent to the carrier, with the filing deadline from the delivery date.
Credits not received. Service credits an SLA audit computed, or credits a
counterparty promised, that the credits ledger shows received short or not at all.
Short-pays not taken. An invoice the rate-confirmation audit found overbilled
that accounts payable paid in full.
Concealed-damage windows. Goods signed for subject to inspection with no
inspection recorded, and the notice window your terms state.

Each event points to the recovery card that already drafts the claim: the OS&D
report, the notice of intent, the rate-confirmation audit or the SLA audit. The
claim is approved there, in the existing claims recovery flow.
What it reads
Receiving (OS&D) records, the claims feed, dispute correspondence, carrier invoices
with their rate confirmations, SLA scorecards, and two ledgers you tag as evidence
sources: accounts-payable payments and credits. Where the ledger an event rests on is
not connected, that event is not reported: a record nobody looked for is not
evidence that it does not exist.
What it produces

A CLAIMS_LEAKAGE evidence document per event on Actionable Twins (claims play), with the evidence
bundle of the recovery card it points to, the amount at stake computed from cited
records, and the earliest deadline with the rule that set it.
From ReviewClaimsLeakage: the events due within a horizon you choose (past-due
first), the total the cards state, and, if you ask, a drafted next step per event.
Each step uses one of five actions (open the recovery draft, follow up a credit,
review a short-pay, schedule an inspection, escalate to a claims handler) and names
its approver.

Human oversight

A claims handler or accounts-payable manager approves every recovery on the card it
points to. Approval seals the evidence document; rejection needs a reason.
The agent never files or serves a claim, sends a notice, takes a short-pay or
deduction, or pays anything.
A computed deadline is an input for the person deciding, not legal advice.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
The agent orders the events and phrases the next step.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. Your records reach the model as fenced,
untrusted data. See Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Never invents a figure. A missing amount is shown as not stated, never as zero.
Refuses to inflate a recoverable amount or move a delivery date or deadline.
Refuses to file, serve or deduct without the approver.
Refuses to waive recovery against a favoured or related party.
Each drafted step is checked by these rules as output, before it reaches you.

How to read its results

It works from your records. A credit or payment that is not in a connected ledger
cannot be seen, so "not received" is only reported when the ledger is connected.
A concealed-damage window is calendared only when your terms state one.
Identified money is not recovered money. Only what a counterparty pays back or
credits is recovered.

docs/user-guide/agents/freight-market-an.title: Freight market analyst
docs/user-guide/agents/freight-market-an.body:
Freight market analyst

Agent: the freight market analyst (freight_market), run from the Freight
market card on Why (/simulate?tab=knowledge&card=freight). The old
/market_diligence address redirects to that card.
What it does
It benchmarks each of your lanes against that lane's own history, and suggests
re-bid, consolidation and fuel-surcharge reviews for your procurement team to
decide. Its jobs:

Rate trend. The median linehaul rate per mile or kilometre over the last 90
days of a lane's records, against the 275 days before. A lane above its own
baseline by more than your target, with enough loads in both windows, is
flagged. With no target set, the change is shown and nothing is flagged.
Seasonal comparison. The same 90 days a year earlier, so a seasonal peak is
not mistaken for a trend.
Tender rejections. How many of your tenders on the lane were rejected.
Fuel surcharge against diesel. How your fuel surcharge per distance moved
against the US EIA weekly diesel price over the same weeks.
Transit and accessorials. Mean transit days, on-time share against planned
transit, and accessorial charges per load.
Candidates. Re-bid candidates (above own trend, or many rejections),
consolidation candidates (thin lanes from one origin to one destination region),
and fuel-surcharge reviews.

What it reads
Your own lane history: the loads and tenders your systems record, with origin,
destination, dates, tender outcome, linehaul, fuel surcharge, accessorials,
distance and its unit, and transit days. A connection is marked as lane history by
the operator.
Two public sources, as context:

US EIA weekly retail on-highway diesel price (U.S. Energy Information
Administration, public domain).
BTS Freight Transportation Services Index (U.S. Bureau of Transportation
Statistics, public domain), shown as national context only.

What it produces

Lane benchmarks with every figure, the windows they cover and the number of loads
behind them.
Flags with the figures that raised them.
Recommended actions, each naming the Transportation Procurement Manager as the
person who decides.
The list of sources consulted, each marked live, cached, stale or not checked,
with its retrieval time, and the rows of your records that could not be used and
why.
On request, a short written summary. It phrases the figures above and adds none.

Human oversight

Every recommended action is a draft. Sending one for approval puts it in the
approval queue, where a named person approves or rejects it.
Approving records the decision. FACE contacts no carrier, sends no tender and
awards no freight.

Model
The optional summary uses the general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. The two public sources are fetched for every organisation, unless the
deployment has turned live public data off. They are cached
with their retrieval time; nothing from your records is sent to them. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

The comparison is your own history plus public fuel data. It uses no proprietary
rate index and refuses to make up a market or spot rate.
Refuses to steer a re-bid or consolidation towards a favoured carrier.
Recommends only. It does not book, tender, award or pay.
A written summary that states a figure the analysis did not compute, or proposes
an action outside its allowed set, is not shown.

How to read its results

A lane is measured against its own history. A lane above its own trend is not
proof it is above the market.
The BTS index covers all US freight. It is context, not a lane benchmark.
A fuel surcharge moving faster than diesel is a reason to check your contract's
fuel table, not proof of an error.
A row without a linehaul rate, a distance or a distance unit is not used, and is
counted with the reason. Nothing is filled in.
With no network or no permission to reach the public sources, the lane figures
still work; the fuel comparison is marked not checked.

Thresholds
There are no built-in thresholds. Each is a target set for a deployment, or for your
organisation by an admin under Admin → Public registries & market data. Until a
target is set, the figure it would judge is shown as measured, nothing is flagged on
it, and the result names it as having no target. Every result shows the thresholds
it applied.



Threshold
Default




Lane above its own baseline by more than
No target set


Tender rejection share that flags a lane
No target set


Fewest tenders before the rejection share counts
No minimum


Fuel surcharge moving beyond the EIA diesel average by more than (points)
No target set


Loads per 30 days below which lanes sharing a region are proposed for consolidation
No target set

docs/user-guide/agents/self-healing/.title: Self-healing
docs/user-guide/agents/self-healing/.body:
Self-healing

Agent: the self-healing agent, which watches FACE's own health and the endpoints FACE
depends on.

Note: This agent acts on its own. It is the one FACE agent whose remediations run
without a person approving each one, so that FACE recovers from a fault in seconds
rather than waiting for someone to be paged. An operator can switch automatic
remediation off with a deployment setting; it is on by default. See
Configuration.

What it does
It receives one health event at a time and picks the single safest remediation from a
fixed list:

Restart a runner or process that has stopped responding.
Trip the circuit breaker to isolate a dependency that keeps failing.
Roll back the most recent change that correlates with the fault.
Scale to add capacity under sustained resource pressure.
Notify a person when no safe automatic fix exists or the fault is ambiguous.

What it reads
A health event describing a degraded in-process resource (CPU, memory, goroutines, a
panic) or an unreachable external endpoint.
What it produces
One remediation from the list above, the target it applies to, a one-line rationale and
a confidence between 0 and 1. A low-confidence or ambiguous case always becomes a
notification for a person, not an action.
Human oversight

Automatic remediation is limited to the five actions above. It can never delete data,
shut a host down or disable a security control (authentication, TLS or the circuit
breaker itself).
Every remediation is logged.
Operators can turn automatic remediation off for the whole deployment, which narrows
the agent to unhealthy-endpoint events.
Everything else FACE recommends still waits for the named approver.

Model
Runs on the deployment's general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
Inside your FACE deployment, on the deployment's own inference. Health events stay in
your deployment; no outside AI service is involved.
Guardrails

A fixed list of permitted actions; anything else is refused.
Unsure means notify, never act.
No destructive or irreversible action, and no change to security controls.
Requests and responses are screened by FACE's guardrails like every other agent.

How to read its results

It handles one event at a time. Causes that span several services are for a person
to read from the notification and the log.
A rollback reverts the most recent change that correlates with the fault, which is not
always the cause.

docs/user-guide/agents/counterparty-back.title: Counterparty background check
docs/user-guide/agents/counterparty-back.body:
Counterparty background check

Agent: the counterparty check (counterparty_check), run from the
Counterparty background check card on Why
(/simulate?tab=knowledge&card=counterparty; &name= starts the check with a business
name). The old /market_diligence address redirects to that card.
What it does
It runs business due diligence on a carrier, broker, freight forwarder, shipper or
consignee from public registries and sanctions lists, and from your own history
with that business. It produces findings for a person to review, never a rating.
Its jobs:

Operating authority. Whether the US motor carrier or broker authority is
active, and whether a revocation is pending.
Insurance on file. Liability insurance against the required minimum, and
cargo insurance or a broker's bond where one is required.
Safety and orders. The published safety rating and any out-of-service order in
force.
Authority age. When the authority was first granted. A very new authority on a
high-value load is a red flag.
Sanctions screening. The business name and the registered names against the
OFAC SDN list, the EU consolidated list and the UK Sanctions List.
Company registries. Legal name, status and registration from GLEIF (by LEI),
SEC EDGAR (by CIK) and UK Companies House (by company number): an inactive or
lapsed entity, a company in liquidation or dissolved, an insolvency history, a
recently incorporated company, and a registered name that differs from the one
given.
Exclusions. Active SAM.gov exclusions (debarment or suspension), by Unique
Entity ID.
Your own history. Loads, on-time share, claims and disputes with this business
in your records.

What it reads

US FMCSA public carrier data (company census, licensing and insurance,
authority history, out-of-service orders), by the USDOT or MC number you give.
OFAC SDN list (U.S. Treasury), the EU consolidated financial sanctions list
(European Commission) and the UK Sanctions List (FCDO), downloaded in full and
screened on the deployment.
GLEIF Legal Entity Identifier records (CC0), SEC EDGAR company submissions
(U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission), UK Companies House company profiles
(Open Government Licence) and SAM.gov exclusions (U.S. General Services
Administration), each by the identifier you give.
Your own lane history and account records.

These registries were chosen because each is public, free, usable commercially, has
an API keyed by an identifier, and registers companies. Where a registry can also
hold a person (an LEI registered to a sole proprietor, an individual EDGAR filer),
the record is reported only as such, with no name. Court dockets are not consulted.
A source that is not given an identifier, or whose API key is not configured on your
deployment, is listed as not checked with that reason.
What it produces

Findings, each with its source, a link to check it, and when it was retrieved.
Red flags among them: revoked or inactive authority, insurance below the required
minimum, an unsatisfactory safety rating, an out-of-service order, a very new
authority on a high-value load, and any sanctions name match.
Sanctions matches, always shown as a possible match that needs human review.
Every source considered, including the ones not checked and why.
At most one recommended action: a review by the Compliance Manager.
The thresholds it applied.

Human oversight

The check decides nothing. A person reviews the findings and decides whether to
work with the business.
FACE does not block, reject, blacklist or notify anyone.

Not a consumer report
This is business due diligence. It runs on businesses only and has no way to name a
private individual. It is not a consumer report, and it must not be used to make or
support decisions about any person's credit, employment, housing or insurance. A
name match on a sanctions list is not an identification: only a person can confirm
or dismiss it.
Model
The findings are read from coded registry fields and computed on the deployment. No
model decides them.
The optional summary uses the general reasoning tier.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. Registries are contacted for every organisation, unless the deployment has
turned live public data off. The only values sent are the
identifiers you typed: USDOT, MC, LEI, CIK, UK company number or SAM.gov UEI.
Sanctions lists are downloaded whole and screened locally, so the business name never
leaves the deployment. SAM.gov and Companies House need a free API key, configured
per deployment as a secret; the key is never shown, logged or passed to a model.
Everything fetched is cached with its retrieval time. See
Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

Refuses a check on a private individual, or for a decision about a person's
credit, employment, housing or insurance.
Refuses protected characteristics as a factor.
Refuses to hide, drop or clear a sanctions match or a red flag.
Never labels a business fraudulent or criminal and never blacklists it.
Treats everything in a registry record or a list as data. It follows no link and no
instruction found there, and a summary is withheld when the material carries one.

How to read its results

Registry data is what the registry published at the time shown and can lag reality.
A clean result does not establish that a business is legitimate, and no name match
does not clear anyone.
FMCSA covers US motor carriers, brokers and forwarders. For a shipper or consignee
those sources are marked not applicable.
Each registry is checked by identifier (USDOT, MC, LEI, CIK, UK company number or
SAM.gov UEI). Enter the identifier to check that registry.
A SAM.gov result labelled "not verified against the live API" comes from a
deployment where the first SAM.gov call has not yet completed and been read. An answer FACE cannot read (an error
page, an unexpected or partial response) is shown as not checked, never as "no
exclusions".

Thresholds
The checks consider how recently an operating authority or company was
established, whether a load is high-value, and the claims ratio and on-time share
in your own records. There are no built-in cut-offs: each is a target set for a
deployment, or for your organisation by an admin under Admin → Public
registries & market data. Until one is set, the figure is shown as a finding that
says no target is set, and nothing is raised for review on it.

docs/user-guide/agents/fraud-detection/.title: Fraud indicators
docs/user-guide/agents/fraud-detection/.body:
Fraud indicators

Agent: the fraud indicator agent (fraud_detection in ExecuteLoop), with the
FRAUD_INDICATOR_REVIEW evidence document and the ReviewFraudIndicators call.
What it does
It flags records in your own logistics and claims data that a claims or
special-investigations reviewer should check, and drafts the check. It never
accuses anyone. It looks across invoices, payments, claims, deliveries, carrier
records, payee details and returns for irregularities that warrant a check.
What it reads
Payments, claims, carrier invoices with their rate confirmations, receiving (OS&D)
records, tracking telemetry and returns records. Everything is keyed by a business
record: an invoice, a payment, a claim, a load, a carrier, a payee or a returns
account.
What it produces

A FRAUD_INDICATOR_REVIEW evidence document per indicator on Actionable Twins (claims play): the
evidence behind it, each item citing its records, the checks that agree and their
weight, a likelihood band (low, medium or high) when you have set band cut-offs,
the amount on the flagged records where one is stated, and one next check.
From ReviewFraudIndicators: the indicators at or above a band you choose, and, if
you ask, a drafted check per indicator. Each check is a concrete verification step
and names its reviewer. An indicator with no band is always listed.

How the likelihood band is set
The band is the checks' weight against the cut-offs you set (band_medium_at and
band_high_at). There are no built-in cut-offs: until you set both, an indicator
shows its checks and weight and says no review cut-offs are set, with no band and no
priority. Every card states the review settings in
force and where they came from.
The statistical checks flag values that are outliers against the rest of the data.
Review settings
The review settings can be adjusted for your deployment with a JSON thresholds
file that names only the values you
change. A file that cannot be read or is out of range is not applied, and every card
says the override was invalid. Band cut-offs are set as a pair, or not at all.
Human oversight

A named claims or special-investigations reviewer decides each indicator, with one
of two choices. Dismiss needs a reason, which is recorded. Escalate opens an
investigation case for that reviewer. Both are written to the decision log. An
indicator is never "approved".
The agent never accuses anyone, never holds, blocks or denies a payment, claim or
refund, and never contacts the party named.
An indicator is not for sending to the party it names.

Model
The deployment's general reasoning tier.
The indicators, bands and amounts are fixed rules and statistics over cited records.
The agent orders the indicators and phrases the next check; the server takes bands
and amounts from the card, and every drafted step is checked before you see it.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own model plane: Runink's shared machines on a Trial, your
own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside AI service is called on any
plan. Your records reach the model as fenced,
untrusted data. See Facts shared by every card.
Guardrails

No profiling: it never uses or infers gender, race, ethnicity, religion,
nationality, age, disability, a name, an address or a neighbourhood.
Never looks into anyone's private life, social media, family, criminal record or
credit.
Refuses to label anyone a fraudster or as guilty, and refuses to hold or deny a
payment without a person.
Refuses to hide or drop an indicator for a particular party.
Each drafted check is screened against these rules as output, before it reaches
you.

How to read its results

This is not a consumer report. It must not be used for decisions about an
individual's credit, employment or insurance.
It works from your records. A pattern can have an innocent explanation the records
do not show, which is why every indicator ends in a check, not a conclusion.

docs/user-guide/agents/customer-analysis.title: Customer analysis
docs/user-guide/agents/customer-analysis.body:
Customer analysis

Agent: the customer analysis (customer_analysis), run from the Customer
analysis card on Why (/simulate?tab=knowledge&card=customers). The old
/market_diligence address redirects to that card.
What it does
It analyses your shipper and consignee business accounts from your own records and
suggests re-pricing, service-level and account reviews for a person to decide. Its
jobs:

Cost to serve and margin. Activity-based cost to serve per account: transport,
warehousing, handling, order processing, returns and other costs, as your records
state them, with the margin on the orders that state both revenue and a cost.
Service. OTIF (on time and in full) per account.
Claims and disputes. Claim and dispute rates per account.
Payment behaviour. Days from invoice to payment, weighted by amount, and open
receivables.
Concentration. Each account's share of revenue, the top-three share and the
Herfindahl-Hirschman index.
Churn signals. Order volume falling, no recent orders, service levels falling
and disputes rising, each with the figures behind it.

What it reads
Your own account records: one row per order, with the account, its type, dates,
revenue, activity costs, delivery outcome, claims, disputes and invoice and payment
dates. A connection is marked as account records by the operator. No public data is
used.
What it produces
