the follow-up flows you own, with their runs, their chat and the proposals made for you;
the scenarios, items and terms you typed into the scenario builder;
the mailbox connections you started and did not finish;
the brief suggestions you dismissed;
the spreadsheets you attached on the Ask page;
on your device: the cached data and your saved role.

You are signed out on every device first, then your data is deleted, then the account
record. Earlier encrypted versions of these records stay in FACE's storage history until it
is compacted and cleaned, which is scheduled for about a day later; nobody can read them
without FACE's key. A personal brief you saved keeps a code derived from your account and is
not deleted yet.
What your organisation keeps
What belongs to your organisation is not yours personally and stays: briefs, personas,
connections, schedules, the run history, the mailbox your organisation connected, the
follow-up tasks flows created, the audit log and the decision records.
You are not named in them afterwards. Where a retained record names you (a task you
finished, a persona you edited, a decision you made), it shows a fixed code,
former-member- and ten characters, instead: the same code for the same person every
time. The decision log is not rewritten: its stored entries keep an
anonymous account number that no longer links to any account or email address, and the
code is shown where the log is read.
One audit entry records that the deletion happened: when, which classes of data, and a
hash standing for the account. It holds no content and no address.
Not reached by the in-app deletion
An older copy of FACE’s sign-in table, from before FACE moved its storage, is keyed by
your email address and is not reached by the in-app deletion. An operator removes it on request:
write to contact@runink.org from your sign-in address.
After the deletion: the access list is not edited
FACE's access list is built from add-users requests that FACE itself cannot change. Deleting
your account does not remove your address from it. If your address is still listed, signing
in with Google again creates a new, empty account. To stop that, ask your organisation's
administrator to remove you from the list.
Without the app
If you can no longer open the app, write to contact@runink.org from the address you sign
in with, with the subject Delete my FACE account. The same page is published for the app
stores at runink.org/account-deletion.
To ask for a copy of your data first, write to the same address with the subject Export my
FACE data: there is no in-app export. The app offers this as a link in the delete dialog.
Retrying
Deleting is safe to repeat. If a call fails part-way, you are already signed out, but the
account record goes last, so it is still there: sign in again and repeat the deletion. A
repeat after success deletes nothing more and writes no second audit entry.

docs/user-guide/accessibility/.title: Accessibility and languages
docs/user-guide/accessibility/.body:
Accessibility and languages

FACE works with a keyboard and a screen reader, never relies on colour alone, comes in
light and dark themes, and speaks English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.
Screen readers and the keyboard

Navigation. Each rail entry is a real button. It takes keyboard focus, shows a
visible focus ring, and responds to Enter and Space. Screen readers announce its label
and whether it is the page you are on.
Icon-only buttons. A button without a text label carries a tooltip and a spoken
label. For example, the assistant button is announced as Open FACE AI assistant.
Status changes. Errors and changing states are announced as they happen, such as
the filter notice on Actionable Twins, a list that failed to load, the reject dialog's
character counter, the answer on Ask, and the hand-off to the twins on Options.
The map. On the Map view, On the map lists every placed thing, so a keyboard
can open the same card a tap does.
Reduced motion. When your system asks for reduced motion, FACE stops decorative
animation, such as the rotation of partner messages on the activity card.

Severity is never colour alone
Neighbouring severity colours are too close to tell apart by colour alone, so every
severity mark also has its own shape, and usually its word:



Severity
Glyph




Critical
filled circle with an exclamation mark


High
warning triangle


Medium
square


Low
dash


OK
check mark



Other states work the same way:

Rule verdicts on Why pair a glyph with the words
Aligned, Drift, Shadow, Missing and Unrated.
How a scenario ended on Options is an icon and
a word.
Remediation banners and audit rows print their status word beside the glyph.

Light and dark themes
FACE has separate light and dark themes, each designed for contrast in its own right.
Choose under Settings › Account, next to Theme:
Light, Dark or System, which follows your device. This device remembers your
choice.
Languages
FACE is available in English, French, Spanish and Portuguese. Under
Settings › Account:

Interface language sets the language of the app's screens. The interface switches
at once.
Agent language sets the language the agent listens and reads its answers aloud in,
and the language FACE writes its answers in.

Some text is not translated: technical identifiers, and text that comes word for word
from a server or a source system. FACE marks where a server's own reply is shown.

docs/user-guide/troubleshooting/.title: Troubleshooting
docs/user-guide/troubleshooting/.body:
Troubleshooting

FACE tells two situations apart. It could not look: the request failed, so nothing is
known. Or it looked and found nothing: the answer came back and was empty. The messages
below are the exact English wording. Check which of the two a message describes before
you act on it.
Signing in



Message
What it means
What to do




Single sign-on is unavailable — the sign-in service could not be reached. You can still sign in with your email and password.
The app could not reach the sign-in service's configuration.
Sign in with your email and password, or try again later.


The server did not accept these credentials.
The email or password was rejected.
Check both and try again.


Invalid two-factor code
The code from your authenticator was wrong or out of date.
Wait for the next code and enter it.


MFA session expired — please sign in again
The second-factor challenge timed out.
Sign in again from the start.


This account is not authorized for this instance
Your account is valid but has no access to this instance.
Access is granted by Runink: ask your Runink contact or your FACE administrator. See Access and the trial.


Session expired — please sign in again
Your session ended.
Sign in again.



No data yet



Message
What it means
What to do




Nothing is connected yet
No data source is attached to this instance, so there is nothing to assess.
Add one under Settings › Integrations › Systems.


No data source is configured yet.
The source list was read and is empty.
Select Connect a data source.


Could not load your data sources.
The source list could not be read.
Select Retry.


Your operation's story starts with a fetch
No run is selected, so the page has nothing to show.
Ask a question on Ask, or select Open an earlier run.


Run a fetch first — the compliance twin analyzes that instance’s real findings, not a blank prompt.
The remediation screens analyse a run's findings, and none has finished yet.
Run a question on Ask first.


Unable to Assess
The twin answered, but could not produce an assessment. This is not a clean result.
Read the summary for the reason. Usually you need to connect a data source and run again.



Ask



Message
What it means
What to do




Switched off: not read by Fetch
An admin switched this connection off, so no run reads it.
Ask an admin to switch it back on, under How FACE knows this on Ask.


{name} was not switched: {error}
The Active switch could not be saved.
Read the reason. Only an admin can switch a connection or runner.


Offline mode: Fetch task queued for background synchronization.
The app could not reach the server, so it kept the run on your device.
Nothing. The run is sent when the connection returns.


Offline queueing failed: {error}
The run could not even be queued.
Try again once you are back online.


No result received
The run ended without a final answer.
Open the run to read what arrived, then ask again.


Your last fetch failed.
The last run did not complete.
Select Open the run and read Result and Error.


Your last fetch answered, but not every phase finished.
The answer came back, and a phase after it did not finish. The message names which, and why.
Pages that phase feeds say so for this run. Ask again, or open an earlier Successful run.


Failed to load fetch starters
The prepared questions could not be loaded.
Type your question instead.


This run is no longer in your history.
The run was deleted from this device.
Run it again.



Options, Why and Actionable Twins



Message
What it means
What to do




Failed to fetch action queue: {error}
The decisions on Actionable Twins could not be read. The list may not be empty.
Select Refresh.


The map could not be loaded: {reason}
The Map view could not read where your assets are.
Read the reason, then open the Map view again.


Live layers could not be read: {reason}
The map's live connection layers could not be read. Your own assets may still show.
Check the connections are active, then open the Map view again.


That file is too large to analyze (3 MB maximum).
The file for Analyze document is over the limit.
Split or reduce the file.


Could not read that file.
The browser could not read the chosen file.
Pick the file again.


Could not load scenarios
The scenarios could not be read.
Select Retry.


Failed to extract rules: {error}
The rules could not be read.
Select Retry on Why.


The options could not be compared: {error}
Options could not compare the options for a decision. Nothing is shown in their place.
Try again.



Automated analysis



Message
What it means
What to do




Automated analysis is starting up…
The analysis models are loading. Everything else works now.
Wait, then select Check again.


Automated analysis is not ready — features that need it are unavailable.
The analysis service cannot answer.
Select Check again. If it persists, see Operating FACE.



Voice



Message
What it means
What to do




Voice input is unavailable in this browser or the microphone was blocked. Type your question instead.
The browser has no speech support, or microphone access was refused.
Allow the microphone for FACE's site in your browser settings, or type instead.



Still stuck
For problems on the deployment side, see Operating FACE.

part of it: Runink deploys and operates FACE for you.

docs/admin-guide/access-and-trial/.title: Access and the trial
docs/admin-guide/access-and-trial/.body:
Access and the trial

Who can sign in
FACE has no public sign-up. Only accounts Runink has approved can sign in, with an
email and password or with Google single sign-on where your deployment offers it.
Anyone else is refused at sign-in, and a public form only records a request to be
contacted.

Access is granted by Runink. To add a person, ask your Runink contact. There is
no invitation form, members list or role editor in the FACE app.
Administrators are added by Runink too. No page in FACE promotes anyone; the
Admin page says so.
Roles. An approved person has one role: Viewer (reads), Editor (works with the data:
asks, briefs, decisions, within what each card's approval rule allows) or
Admin (also the Admin page: guard rules, external-search names, thresholds,
standing rules and the decision log). The server checks the role on every call.
Suppliers. A supplier contact can be approved with the supplier role and one
party. It sees only the orders addressed to that party, and every change it makes
arrives as a proposal a named person approves. There is no guest link.

The trial
The trial lasts 14 days, then the workspace is read-only: nothing is deleted, and
everything stays readable. Access to a trial is granted by Runink, like any other
access. Trials are the same for everyone.
After the trial
Buying a plan lifts the read-only state. Plans and prices are on the FACE product page
at runink.org; to buy one, contact Runink.
Settings › Subscription shows the plan Runink recorded for your organisation. FACE
takes no payment inside the app and does not charge by usage.
Availability
FACE is not generally available yet. The web app exists; the Android app is built but
not published on Google Play; the iOS app is not built; there is no Google Cloud
Marketplace listing. Runink FACE is sold separately from Runink TIDDE (Trusted Intelligence for Developer &
Data Experience), Runink PULSE (Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine) and Runink LUNA
(Lifestyle Understanding & Navigation Assistant), and the Runink
platform layer it runs on ships with it.

docs/admin-guide/admin-page/.title: Admin page
docs/admin-guide/admin-page/.body:
The Admin page

Admin (/admin) holds the settings that govern FACE itself for your organisation:
its guard rules, what may be searched outside, the thresholds the market agents apply,
the standing rules and the decision log. It does not manage people: who may sign in,
and with which role, is set by Runink (see Access and the trial).
Open Settings at the foot of the rail. The Account tab has an Admin card with the
Admin entry, shown only when the server reports that you are an admin of the
organisation. The server checks your role again on every call, so the page cannot
be used by someone without it.

Administrators
The page opens with Administrators are set by the platform, not on this page. Ask
Runink to add an administrator. There is no members list, invitation form or role
editor in FACE, and no page promotes anyone.
Grounding gate
GROUNDING GATE holds FACE's own guard rules: the rules every agent call runs
through (the OpenBias and injection rule sets). They govern the application, not your
business, so they live here and not on Why. Your business rules are on
Why.

Show the {count} rules lists the rule inventory with each rule's CATEGORY,
RULE and SEVERITY. Hide rules folds it away.
Type a term or hypothesis and select Check this text. It is checked against the
same rules that guard the agent call. Nothing is sent and nothing is logged. The
result reads No rule fired or Would be refused, with how many rules were
evaluated. Not checked yet means nothing was checked; The check couldn’t run
means it failed.

There is no "percent grounded": a rule fires or it does not. Only an admin sees the gate, and every use is audited.
External web search
External web search is always on. Only a query a person types, or one of the
confirmed public names an admin lists here (carriers, ports, competitors), is sent to
public search engines; a query built from your data is made only from those names, and
only when the text mentions them. Schema, table, column and row content never is. Each
result says whether an external source was consulted, and which.
Public registries and market data
Public registries & market data are always on. The market and due-diligence agents
contact public registries and statistics with the identifiers a person types, and
nothing from your records; each result names every source, its publisher, licence and
retrieval time. An operator can turn live public data off for a whole deployment, for
example an air-gapped one; each source then says it was not checked, and why.
Thresholds for this organisation sets the limits those agents apply. There are no
built-in limits: a field neither your deployment nor your organisation has set reads
No target set, and the agents show that figure as measured and flag nothing on it.
The same list holds the cycle-service level a site's safety stock is sized for
(for example 0.95). With none set, the site page computes no safety stock or reorder
point, and says the level is not set.
Every change to the public names or the thresholds is audited with its author.
Standing rules
Standing rules lists the decisions made into policy: Decisions made into policy.
Each takes effect only after a second, different admin approves the exact text; any
admin can revoke it. A rule is proposed from an approved card on
Actionable Twins.

Each rule shows its conditions (a later card must match all of them), its tier
(Guarded — one named approver or Autonomous — runs with no approver), who
proposed it and its state: Awaiting second approval, Active or Revoked.
Approve rule approves the exact text. The proposer cannot approve their own rule.
Revoke ends a rule. Any admin can revoke one.
No standing rule has been proposed. means the list is empty. Standing rules
cannot be read, so none is in effect means the read failed, and then no standing
rule applies.

If the standing rules cannot be read, none is in effect, and the instance policy alone decides. Where the instance policy and a standing rule both match, the stricter one wins.
Decision log
Decision log lists every approval, rejection, refusal and outcome. Each record names the card and who decided. Chain verified ✓ ({count} records) confirms the log is intact; Chain broken at record {seq} names where it is not. No decisions recorded yet. means the log is empty; a failed read says the log
is unknown, not empty.
RPCs behind this page

MetasearchService.EvaluateBias, ListBiasRules, for the grounding gate.
TwinsService.ListStandingRules, ApproveStandingRule, RevokeStandingRule, for the
standing rules.

See the API reference.

docs/admin-guide/data-sources/.title: Data sources
docs/admin-guide/data-sources/.body:
Data sources

FACE starts from the systems you already run: warehouses and databases, ERPs and
SaaS platforms, files and buckets, event buses, telemetry from pallets, readers and
trucks, and camera feeds. You add each one as a connection in
Settings › Integrations › Systems, then choose it as a source on Ask or in a
brief. Every connection must be encrypted, with a login where the protocol has one:
FACE refuses one that is not.
This section describes each connector: the settings a connection takes, how
credentials are held, what Test checks, and what Explore and Sample return.
Live connection types (cameras, sensors, field readers) open their live view from the
connection's card on Ask. See Connections and credentials.
How to read this section
Every connector page answers the same four questions:

Which type spellings resolve. FACE lowercases the connection type and
strips spaces, underscores and hyphens before looking it up, so Service Now,
service-now and servicenow are the same type.
Which settings and credentials it reads. Settings are ordinary fields on the
connection record. Secrets are kept in a sealed credential bundle and are
never returned. See Connections and credentials.
What Test does. Some connectors dial the source. Others can only save the
configuration. The response tells you which through live_check_performed,
and each page says what a successful probe does not establish.
What Explore and Sample return. Explore reads catalogue metadata only.
Sample reads a bounded set of real rows, one dataset at a time. See
Explore, sample and profile.

Connector families

Connections and credentials: Where to add and choose them, security rules, credentials, Test semantics
Quickstarts: The quickstart estate: a dataset to load and fetch for 32 of the 36 connection types, and every connector at once
Explore, sample and profile: What metadata is read, and which values may leave a source
SQL warehouses and databases: Snowflake, Databricks, PostgreSQL, MySQL
Enterprise SaaS and ERP: SAP, Salesforce, Guidewire, ServiceNow, Google Workspace
Files and object storage: Excel, CSV/JSON/Parquet objects, S3, GCS, Azure Blob, document sources
Streaming: Kafka: Topic catalogue and Schema Registry
Event listeners: Changes from PostgreSQL and Kafka that trigger analysis
Telemetry: MQTT 3.1.1 over TLS, RFID (LLRP and REST), GPS, Modbus-TCP
Logistics systems of record: OMS, TMS, WMS, YMS, IMS, WHS and more over REST
CCTV and video: RTSPS, ONVIF over HTTPS, snapshots, device capture
Flipper edge reader: Handheld field readings through the edge agent
Web and crawler: One page as text, and bounded crawls
Runners: Where queries run, and keeping data in your network
Networking and address policy: IPv6-first, Happy Eyeballs, refused addresses
Troubleshooting: The errors connectors return, and what to do

Implementation principles

Every connection is encrypted. TLS with the certificate checked, and a login
where the protocol has one. A connection that does not meet this cannot be saved,
and a stored one is refused until it is upgraded. See
Security requirements.
Wire protocols are implemented natively. MQTT, LLRP, Modbus-TCP, the Kafka
handshake, RTSP and ONVIF are written directly against the wire format. FACE adds no
third-party protocol library for them.
An empty answer is never a silent success. When a telemetry or
system-of-record connector connects and receives nothing, it reports
Success=false and names what it listened to. It does not return an empty table.
Absence stays absent. When a source does not state a threshold, a unit or a
row count, FACE leaves the value unset. It does not fill in a plausible default.
Every read is bounded. Every connector caps its collection windows, record
counts, page counts and body sizes. When a read hits a cap, the result is
marked as truncated.
Observed lineage records structure only. Every extraction through the
connector registry writes a lineage record with column names, counts, durations
and a query shape. The record never includes result values or credentials.

docs/admin-guide/data-sources/connection.title: Connections and credentials
docs/admin-guide/data-sources/connection.body:
Connections and credentials

You add a connection once, in Settings › Integrations › Systems, and then choose
it as a source wherever you ask a question: on Ask, and per brief on Briefs.
FACE refuses any connection that would send data or a credential unencrypted.
Where you add and choose connections



What you want
Where




Add, edit or remove a connection
Settings › Integrations › Systems. New connection opens the connection wizard. A connection that an answer on Ask proposed opens there too, ready to confirm.


Add, edit or remove a runner
Settings › Integrations › Runners. See Runners.


Choose the sources for a question
Ask. Each connection is a card that reads Included in fetch or Not included. An admin can also switch a source Active or Inactive. An inactive source reads Switched off: not read by Fetch.


Choose the sources for a brief
Briefs, in the brief's editor. Each run reads the connections ticked there. With all ticked, it reads every connection, including ones added later. A brief that reads nothing cannot be saved.


Watch a live source
The connection's own card on Ask (see below).



Live connection types have a view of their own. It opens from that connection's card
on Ask, with the connection already chosen:



Connection type
Views on its card




MQTT, sensor gateway, GPS telematics, RFID reader
Live sensors, Devices


CCTV, video stream, camera
Surveillance


Flipper Zero field reader
Field reader, Devices



A view opened from a card shows only that connection, with Show all to widen it.
The rest of this page is reference. A connection is made of two things that are
stored apart: a record, which holds settings, and a credential bundle, which
holds secrets. The sections below explain how they are split, stored and replicated,
what the connection RPCs report, and the security every connection must meet.
The connection record
Connection (in face.proto) carries:



Field
Meaning




id
Server-generated when empty (conn_).


name
Display name. It is never used to decide how a connection behaves.


type
The connector type, for example snowflake or mqtt. Matching ignores case, spaces, underscores and hyphens.


environment
Free-form tier label (prod, staging, …). It is not a statement about what stands behind the source.


runner
Which runner executes work for this connection. See Runners.


config
A oneof holding one typed configuration message, for example snowflake, mqtt or logistics_api.


properties
A map of extra non-secret settings. Many connectors read fallbacks from it.


credential_state
Filled by ListConnections (see below).


source_backing
Filled by ListConnections (see below).



Secrets never stay on the record
Several configuration messages still have secret-looking fields (password,
client_secret, personal_access_token, service_account_json, api_key,
security_token). When a connection is created, FACE reads those fields,
moves them into the credential bundle, and never writes them back out. A
connection you read back through ListConnections has those fields empty. That
is by design.
Credentials are stored encrypted and never returned by the API. The internal
record type has no field that can hold a secret, and secrets placed in the
free-form properties map are rejected.
Connectors read their secrets only from the credential bundle they are handed.
Setting a password on the record has no effect.
Connection strings
For snowflake and databricks you can paste a connection string in the
connection_string property. FACE parses it at save time:

The settings it names become typed settings. The string wins for every
setting it states. Settings it does not state keep what the form carried.
The secret it contains goes to the credential bundle under the connector's
normal key. The raw string itself is not kept.
If the string cannot be parsed, the save fails, so you find out when you paste,
not at the next fetch.
For Snowflake, a DSN field that FACE does not carry is refused rather than
dropped silently. So is an explicit host that disagrees with the account.

For other types, a connection_string credential is left in the bundle untouched.
The Azure object store reads it from there.
Security requirements
Every connection must use encrypted transport with the server's certificate checked,
and a login wherever the protocol has one. This is not a setting you can turn off. The
server enforces it in four places:

Save. CreateConnection and updates refuse an insecure connection before anything
is written, with InvalidArgument:
this connection cannot be saved without its security settings: .
Test. TestConnection on a draft that would be refused dials nothing and answers
nothing was dialled: ….
Every read of a stored connection. Fetch, Explore, discovery, data listeners, live
sensors, document ingest and Test all refuse a stored connection that fails the policy,
with FailedPrecondition:
this connection is not secured: ; open it in Settings › Integrations and upgrade its security.
The stored connection is kept as it is. Nothing rewrites or deletes it.
List. ListConnections sets security_ok and security_problems on each
connection. The connection wizard opens a refused connection in Upgrade security.

Each problem is one plain sentence that names the setting or credential to fix.
Rules for every connector type:

insecure_skip_verify is refused.
A cleartext address scheme is refused on every address setting, every Kafka bootstrap
server, and every value in properties: http, ws, tcp, mqtt, rtsp, ftp,
amqp and plaintext. Use https, wss, tls, mqtts, rtsps, ftps or amqps.
An ssl_mode of disable, allow or prefer is refused.
A Kafka security_protocol of plaintext or sasl_plaintext is refused.
A connector type with no security rule cannot be used.

Rules per connector type:



Type
What it needs




Kafka
security_protocol sasl_ssl, sasl_mechanism scram-sha-512 or scram-sha-256, a username and a password credential. ssl alone is refused because it carries no login. The CA is optional (empty means the public roots). A Schema Registry, when set, is https with its own schema_registry_username and schema_registry_password.


PostgreSQL, Redshift, MySQL
ssl_mode stated as require, verify-ca or verify-full (unset is refused), a username and a password credential.


MQTT
A tls://, ssl://, mqtts:// or wss:// broker, use_tls on, a username and a password credential.


RFID
LLRP over TLS (use_tls, or llrps). The REST protocol needs an https endpoint.


GPS telematics
An https endpoint. The nmea provider is refused: it is a raw TCP stream with no encryption.


Sensor gateway
Modbus/TCP over TLS (use_tls, port 802), or an https endpoint.


Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure)
An https endpoint. A bare S3 host:port needs use_tls.


Files
The same as object storage, or an https SharePoint site_url.


Salesforce, Guidewire, SAP, Dynamics 365, SharePoint, ServiceNow, logistics APIs, Flipper and Pineapple agents
https addresses. A bare host that the connector would dial as http is refused.


CCTV and video
rtsps:// or https:// feeds. A device capture or a video file on the server dials nothing.


Web pages
https. A bare address is read as https.


BigQuery, Snowflake, HubSpot, GitHub, Google Workspace, Databricks
https by construction. An explicit http:// is refused.


Excel, documents
No network transport. A file path that is a URL must be https.



Creating, listing and deleting
Create. CreateConnection takes the Connection and a credentials map.
FACE writes the credential bundle first and then the record. If writing the
credentials fails, no connection is created, and the response carries
success: false with the underlying message. The response echoes
connection_id either way, so a retry does not create a second row.
List. ListConnections returns every connection with two annotations and a
warnings list:

credential_state tells you what this node holds:
| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| CREDENTIAL_STATE_PRESENT | A bundle was found and opened on this node. Nothing was dialled, so an expired password still reads PRESENT. |
| CREDENTIAL_STATE_NONE_NEEDED | The catalogue says this type reads no secret, for example Excel. This is a normal state. |
| CREDENTIAL_STATE_ABSENT | There is no bundle for a type that expects one. FACE cannot tell "never entered" apart from "not present on this node". |
| CREDENTIAL_STATE_UNREADABLE | A bundle exists and could not be opened. Re-entering the credential does not fix a key problem. |
| CREDENTIAL_STATE_UNSPECIFIED | Not computed. This value is not "present" or "absent". |
The fetch pipeline uses the same classifier, so the list and a fetch always
agree. Opening a present bundle is recorded in the credential audit trail.

source_backing is covered below.

warnings carries plain-language conditions about the list itself, such as
storage durability. Show them as written. They are not failures.

Delete. DeleteConnection answers with an explicit outcome:



outcome
Meaning




DELETE_CONNECTION_OUTCOME_DELETED
The credential bundle was removed first, then the record.


DELETE_CONNECTION_OUTCOME_NOT_FOUND
This instance holds no such id. Nothing was deleted.


DELETE_CONNECTION_OUTCOME_FAILED
The delete was attempted and failed. message carries the error, and the connection may still exist. An empty id also returns this, with no connection id provided.



success is true only for DELETED. Deleting a connection does not revoke the
credential at its issuer, and it does not rewrite fetch definitions or lineage
that reference the id.
Test: what live_check_performed means 
ConfigService.TestConnection resolves the connector for the connection's type:

If the connector has a live probe, FACE runs it with the stored credentials.
If the connector has no live probe, FACE says so and does not claim a result.

Always read the two booleans together, never the message text:



success
live_check_performed
Meaning
Typical message




true
true
The connector dialled the source, and the source answered and accepted the credential.
Connectivity verified


true
false
The configuration is stored. Nothing was verified. The type has no live probe.
Configuration saved — a live connectivity check isn't implemented yet for this source type


false
true
The probe ran and failed. message is the connector's own error.
varies (see Troubleshooting)


false
false
The connection could not be resolved.
Connection not found, Unknown connection type "…", could not read the connection: …



A successful probe establishes reachability and credential acceptance, and
nothing more. It does not establish any of the following:

that a sensor is publishing
that an antenna is attached
that a probe is calibrated
that the credential has scope for any other resource
that any records exist

Each connector page lists exactly what its probe does.
Source backing
source_backing states what stands behind a connection on this instance. It
is computed from the connection's address and dials nothing.



Value
Meaning
What it does not establish




SOURCE_BACKING_LIVE
Nothing that FACE ships stands in for this connection. Whatever it addresses is what it reads.
That the source exists, is reachable, or works. A connection to a host that does not exist is still LIVE and simply fails.


SOURCE_BACKING_UNSPECIFIED
Not computed. Every RPC other than ListConnections leaves it unset.
Anything about the connection. It is the absence of an answer, not a "live" one.



When a connector fails, the failure is reported as a failure. FACE never substitutes
other rows for a failed source. environment is not a substitute for this field: it is
a free-form label for the tier of your estate a connection points at, such as
"prod" or "staging".
Storage and replication

Records are one replicated snapshot per tenant. FACE stores the snapshot in
its own encrypted application filesystem and proposes changes through the
platform's consensus group, so every control-plane replica sees the same set of
connections.
Credential bundles are rows in the same encrypted store. Each row is sealed
under a key derived for FACE and bound to its path. Bundles do not travel on
the replication log. Only the record snapshot does.
When a fetch runs on a dedicated runner, the control plane reads the bundle once
(an audited read). It then seals the bundle to that runner's in-memory key for
that single dispatch. The runner never writes the credential to disk. See
Runners.

For the encryption and key model, see /docs/architecture/security/.
Observed lineage
Every connector returned by the registry is wrapped by a lineage recorder. Each
extraction appends a record to an append-only log. The record contains:

column names
counts and durations
a literal-free query shape and its fingerprint
a closed-set error class

A record never contains result values, driver messages or credentials.
Camera ingests are recorded separately (one record per ingest, with a row count of
zero, because a camera sends frames rather than rows). Lineage is visible in
source activity. See /docs/concepts/.

docs/admin-guide/data-sources/quickstart.body:
Quickstarts


Warning: The test-estate safety rule: stand the test estate up only beside a test instance, never a production deployment. Its systems are throwaway test services with published credentials: change-me is every test credential. They are still encrypted and still ask for a login, because FACE refuses a connection that is not (see Connector security). Use a scratch machine or a scratch cluster.

FACE by Runink (Fulfilment Autonomous Claims Engine) connects to the systems a logistics team already runs. These quickstarts give 32 of the catalogue's 36 connection types the quickstart estate, a real dataset you can download, load and fetch: one company, Quillmere Freight Lines, written out in each system's native shape, with the model FACE should find in it. The other four types have no quickstart dataset: bimcad (BIM / CAD site-plan drawings under a bucket or SharePoint folder, read through the files connector), flipper (see Flipper edge reader), pineapple (a WiFi Pineapple agent, with the same https rule as Flipper) and webpage (see Web and crawler).
Start with See all connectors at once: it is the walkthrough across every source, and it shows where the evidence for each of the six planted anomalies lives.
What every quickstart page gives you

what the connection is, and its grade;
the setting and credential names from the catalogue, and the test connection's values;
how to stand the test system up;
what FACE finds: the datasets, keys and row counts of the expected model;
how the source joins the shared Quillmere universe, and which planted anomalies it holds evidence for;
a download. Streams link to their replay recordings, never to a file bundle.

Where a quickstart connection goes in FACE

Add it in Settings › Integrations › Systems: select New connection, pick the source, fill in the settings and credentials, choose the runner, then Test & save.
Use it on Ask. Every connection shows as a card among Ask's sources, marked Included in fetch or Not included. An admin can switch a connection Active or Inactive; an inactive one is not read.
Use it in a brief. In the brief's editor on Briefs, tick the connections it reads. With all ticked, it reads every connection, including ones added later. A brief that reads nothing cannot be saved.
Watch a live source. A camera opens Surveillance; an MQTT, IoT, sensor-gateway, GPS or RFID connection opens Live sensors and Devices; a field reader opens Field reader and Devices. Each opens from that connection's card on Ask, already narrowed to it.

Connector security
FACE refuses a connection that would send data, or the login that reads it, unencrypted. It refuses it when you save it, and it refuses again on every read of a stored connection that does not meet the rule. The error names each setting to fix and says to open the connection in Settings › Integrations and upgrade its security. The rule holds for the test estate too, so every test connection on these pages is the secured form.
For every type:

insecure_skip_verify must be off: the server's certificate is always checked.
No address may use a cleartext scheme: http, ws, tcp, mqtt, rtsp, ftp, amqp or plaintext. Use https, wss, tls, mqtts, rtsps, ftps or amqps.
ssl_mode may not be disable, allow or prefer, and a Kafka security_protocol may not be plaintext or sasl_plaintext.

What each type needs on top of that:



Type
Needs




Kafka
security_protocol sasl_ssl; sasl_mechanism scram-sha-512 or scram-sha-256; a username and the password credential. A Schema Registry, when named, is https:// with its own schema_registry_username and schema_registry_password. ssl_ca_pem is optional.


PostgreSQL, Redshift, MySQL
ssl_mode stated as require, verify-ca or verify-full (unset is refused); a username and the password credential.


MQTT, IoT
A tls://, ssl://, mqtts:// or wss:// broker, use_tls on, a username and the password credential.


RFID
LLRP over TLS (use_tls on, or llrps). A reader read over HTTP must use https://.


GPS
An https:// endpoint. Provider nmea is a raw TCP stream with no encryption and is refused.


Sensor gateway
Modbus/TCP over TLS (use_tls on, port 802), or an https:// endpoint.


Object store, files
An https:// endpoint, or use_tls on for a bare S3 host.


CCTV
An rtsps:// or https:// feed. rtsp:// and http:// are refused.


Logistics systems, SAP, Guidewire, field readers
https:// addresses. A bare host is refused, because FACE would dial it unencrypted.


Salesforce, ServiceNow, Dynamics 365, SharePoint, web pages
https:// addresses. A bare host is read as https.


BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, HubSpot, GitHub
Nothing more: their APIs are https by construction.


Excel, Document
Nothing more: nothing is dialled. An Excel file_path that is a URL must be https://.



A type FACE has no security rule for cannot be used.
Grades
Grade each type honestly before you pick one to try.



Grade
Meaning




A
Open source. It stands up locally from the download, with the model and its rows, end to end.


B
The download holds the model. The platform itself needs a vendor account or trial.


C
Model only. There is no freely available local edition of the platform.


D
Dataset and model: the quickstart dataset and its expected model ship. There is no vendor system to stand up for this type; load the dataset and fetch it.

Business apps: Salesforce, SAP, Guidewire, ServiceNow, HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics 365, SharePoint lists, GitHub
Logistics systems: Order management (OMS), Transport management (TMS), Warehouse (WHS), Yard management (YMS), Inventory management (IMS), Inventory, Logistics API
Files: Files, Excel, Document (legacy type), Object store
Streams: Apache Kafka, MQTT, IoT, RFID readers, GPS and telematics, Sensor gateway, CCTV cameras

Downloads
There are 25 zips for 32 connection types, and none is missing. The 7 streaming connectors (cctv, gps, iot, kafka, mqtt, rfid and sensorgateway) are dialled and held open, so they ship as replayable stream recordings under streams//, not as zips. The other 25 types each have one zip.
The downloads live at https://docs.runink.org/downloads/connections/, keyed by connection type, so every Runink product's docs link to the same files. Every download is generated at publish time, from a fixed seed, and scanned before it is published: hosts end in .invalid, addresses are in the documentation ranges, and the only credential value is change-me.

universe.json: the reconciliation graph. Every shared entity, every link between sources, and the six planted anomalies with their evidence.
manifest.json: every download with its size and SHA-256.
SHA256SUMS: the same list, for sha256sum -c.

What these quickstarts are not

Not product data. Nothing in the downloads is read by the FACE backend at runtime, and the product image carries none of it.
Not a deployment. The test estate is made of throwaway test services whose credentials are published. Keep it on a scratch machine.
Not a measurement of every connector. A test compares FACE's discovery with the expected model for PostgreSQL and MySQL. For every other type, the expected model is the shape the source holds, and each page says what FACE reads for that type.

See all connectors at once


Warning: The test-estate safety rule: stand the test estate up only beside a test instance, never a production deployment. Its systems are throwaway test services with published credentials: change-me is every test credential. They are still encrypted and still ask for a login, because FACE refuses a connection that is not (see Connector security). Use a scratch machine or a scratch cluster.

This is the end-to-end walkthrough: one company in every connector, and FACE making sense of all of them together. Every source below is a view of the same company, Quillmere Freight Lines (quillmere.invalid). A shipment in PostgreSQL is the same shipment in the Kafka events, the GPS track, the SAP delivery, the Salesforce case, the claim PDF, the dock-camera frame and the RFID read. Six anomalies are planted across the sources, and each one can only be seen by reading more than one of them.
The universe

There are 23 distinct customer POs for 24 orders. That difference is one of the planted anomalies. universe.json has every entity, every link between sources, and every anomaly with its evidence.
The walkthrough
Connect the sources in this order. Each step adds a kind of source, and each step has something to show.

Connect the two databases FACE reads end to end
Load postgres and mysql into scratch engines and add both connections. Explore returns their tables, columns, types, primary keys and declared foreign keys: the operational system (customers, orders, shipments) and freight billing (carriers, rate contracts, invoices). These two are the ones a test checks against the expected model, so start here.

Add the event bus and the telemetry
Stand up kafka, or the live Kafka estate for a stream that does not end, and use the recordings for mqtt, iot, gps, rfid, sensorgateway and cctv. Kafka shows its topic list and value schemas. Its Schema Registry and ksqlDB add which business domain each topic's schema belongs to, which topic a query computes from which, and which topics carry no traffic. The telemetry sources have no catalogue: FACE collects for a window and infers each feed's shape, and the reader location, the GPS asset_ids and the gateway channels settings tie readings to docks and trailers.

Add the business apps and the systems of record
Add salesforce, sap, guidewire, servicenow, hubspot, d365, sharepoint and github, then the logistics systems: oms, tms, whs, yms, ims, inventory and logisticsapi. Each page says what FACE reads for that type. Where FACE reads no catalogue, open the payload next to its expected model: the shared keys are the same strings.

Add the files
The files dataset lays the estate's files out by the store each would live in: claim and invoice PDFs on S3, dock photos on GCS, dock video on Azure, the carrier rate sheet over SFTP, the scorecard on SharePoint, and an orders export on the runner's disk. The PDFs are real PDF text, the images decode and the clips are MJPEG. Its page names the connection type that reads each store. excel, document and objectstore hold three more small datasets.

Add the cloud warehouses
snowflake, databricks, redshift and bigquery need a cloud account. Load their SQL into an account you own. Against a real account, FACE reads the Snowflake and Databricks catalogues; for Redshift and BigQuery, show the dataset next to its expected model.

Walk the six anomalies
Take them in the order below. Each one names the sources that hold its evidence, the file, and the literal string to look for, so every claim made on screen can be checked against the data.


The six planted anomalies
Each anomaly is the only one of its kind in the universe, and a test re-measures each one from the data. Files inside a zip are named by their path in that zip.
1. A duplicate customer PO (ANOM-4)
Customer PO PO-0002-4194 was accepted twice, as SO-30014 and SO-30015, with identical lines; both shipped.

Warning: The test-estate safety rule: stand the test estate up only beside a test instance, never a production deployment. Its systems are throwaway test services with published credentials: change-me is every test credential. They are still encrypted and still ask for a login, because FACE refuses a connection that is not (see Connector security). Use a scratch machine or a scratch cluster.

Grade A · dataset: SQL (DDL and rows in the engine's dialect) · type postgres
What it is
A PostgreSQL database. In the test estate it is Quillmere's operational system, schema ops: customers and their delivery sites, warehouses (three distribution centres and a retail store), yards and docks; the item master (ops.items: every SKU with its name, category, EAN-13 and the words a camera or OCR reads off it); a year of orders, 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-29 with the 2025 holiday season in it, and the shipments that served them, leg by leg; the fleet, the site and yard equipment with their readings against stated limits, and the maintenance work orders; inventory, reorder policies and replenishment orders; route plans, their stops and their revisions; freight invoices, claims, their evidence and correspondence. The connector reference is SQL warehouses and databases.
Grade
A. Open source. It stands up locally from the download, with the model and its rows, end to end. Any PostgreSQL 13 or later works; the dataset is verified on 16.15.
See the grade table for all 32 types.
Settings and credentials
From the connection catalogue. Settings are ordinary fields on the connection record. Credentials are kept in a sealed bundle and never returned.

Credentials: password. In the test estate, every credential is change-me. Credentials are write-only: they go into the sealed credential bundle and are never returned.
Stand up the test system
The safety rule at the top of this page comes first: a scratch machine or a scratch cluster, never a production or platform one.

Download postgres.zip and unzip it. It holds postgres/01_schema.sql, the rows in postgres/02_data_01.sql to postgres/02_data_16.sql (load them in name order), and postgres/expected.json.
Start a scratch PostgreSQL 13 or later with TLS on, because ssl_mode require needs it. The official image ships a self-signed certificate you can use for a test:
docker run --rm -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me -p 5432:5432 postgres:16 \
  -c ssl=on \
  -c ssl_cert_file=/etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem \
  -c ssl_key_file=/etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key


Create the database and the reader role, then load the schema and the rows, in that order:
psql -h localhost -U postgres -c "CREATE DATABASE quillmere_ops"
psql -h localhost -U postgres -c "CREATE ROLE face_reader LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me'"
psql -h localhost -U postgres -d quillmere_ops -f postgres/01_schema.sql $(for f in postgres/02_data_*.sql; do printf -- '-f %s ' "$f"; done)
psql -h localhost -U postgres -d quillmere_ops -c "GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA ops TO face_reader; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA ops TO face_reader"


Add the connection with the settings above, as Create it in the Console shows. Replace pg.quillmere.invalid with the address of your scratch engine: a .invalid name never resolves.

Create it in the Console
The screens below were taken on a live instance, adding the quickstart's database as Runink hosts it. Your host is your scratch engine's address; every other value is the test connection's.

Open Settings › Integrations › Systems and select New connection.

Details: fill in the settings.
| Field | Value |
|---|---|

| Environment | where this source lives, for example dev or staging |
| Host / endpoint | your engine's address |
| Port | 5432 |
| Database name | quillmere_ops |
| User | face_reader |
| Ssl mode | require (encrypt, do not verify the certificate). Use a verifying mode when the engine's certificate is from a CA your runner trusts. FACE refuses disable, allow, prefer and an unset mode. |


Scroll to Credentials and enter the reader's Password. It is sealed when you save and never shown again.


Runner: keep Runink managed, or pick a registered runner that can reach the engine, then Next.

Review: check the values. Credentials reads none entered until you type the password in step 4. Keep Test after saving ticked and select Test & save.



The new connection appears in the list with a credential stored chip and the test's result. It shows as a source on Ask and in every brief's source list. To read it, see Ask.
What FACE finds
FACE reads the catalogue: information_schema, with the declared primary and foreign keys, every COMMENT ON table, view and column as the dataset's and field's description, and each view's definition (pg_get_viewdef). Partitions and relations an extension owns (such as pg_stat_statements' views) are not listed as datasets; the discovery says how many were left out. A test loads this dataset into an empty engine, runs FACE's discovery, and compares the result with the expected model (TestSynthUniverseDiscoveryMatchesExpected).

The tables of schema recovery (read by the connection postgres-recovery, not by postgres-operations) are described in Dangerous goods and luxury assets; their row counts are the generator's (TestSynthOpsRecoveryTables) and are not restated here.
Every table declares its primary key, and the relations are declared foreign keys: an order to its customer and warehouse, a shipment to its order, origin warehouse, destination site, dock and tractor, a leg and its reefer readings to their shipment, a channel's readings to the channel, a policy and a replenishment order to the supplier's item, a stop to its plan version and shipment, a revision to the plan version it produced and to the revision that triggered it, evidence and messages to their claim. expected.json lists every one.
What the rows let FACE show



Scenario
Tables
What FACE does with them




Routes
shipments (origin_warehouse_id, dest_site_id, status, transport_mode, temp_min_c/temp_max_c), customer_sites (lat/lon)
the run's routes phase draws every pending shipment from its warehouse to its customer site, with the tightest temperature band the routed shipments state


Reactive fulfilment
inventory_positions (on_hand, available, lead_time_days), orders + order_lines
the site page computes safety stock and a reorder point per item from the lead time, the daily demand and the cycle-service level your organisation sets in Admin, and shows the items under it after the last demand spike


Fleet planning
route_stops (a dispatch feed's columns: vehicle_id, stop_sequence, latitude/longitude, demand_kg, vehicle_capacity_kg, planning_speed_kmh, window_start/window_end, temperature_min_c/max_c), vehicles (status, capacity, reefer capability), vehicle_shifts
the fleet planner's stops, beside the GPS fixes of the live fleet topic


Recursive re-plans
route_plan_revisions (trigger_kind, triggered_by_revision_id, legs_before/legs_after)
the history of re-plans, an excursion's re-plan triggering a delay re-plan, a reassignment and the receiving plan's re-plan


Predictive maintenance
site_assets, asset_channels (each limit and its source), asset_readings, maintenance_work_orders
30 days of readings to check a projection against what happened; the live readings are on the Kafka equipment topic


Cold chain
shipment_legs (band per leg), reefer_readings, temperature_excursions
time out of band per leg


Claims
claims, claim_evidence, claim_messages (sent, replied, resolved, closed), remediation_orders
follow a claim from filing to close


Item lookup
items (name, category, aliases, ean), inventory_positions
find an item by the word a detector or OCR produces (teddy bear, pikachu, husky) or by its EAN-13, then its stock at each warehouse


The 2025 holiday season
orders + order_lines from 2025-10-01, replenishment_orders, route_plans, route_plan_revisions
a season to forecast the next from: the toy line's lift from November to Christmas (the teddy bear steady, the Pikachu plush breaking out, the husky plush running out on its 24-day supplier lead time), a smaller lift on household items, the peak-season replenishment orders, and the demand_spike re-plans of Black Friday week and the pre-Christmas peak


The store's window
warehouses (the store ST-NAPERVILLE: Naperville, IL, US, with lat/lon), its orders + order_lines (point-of-sale tickets), inventory_positions, replenishment_orders, items, supplier_items
a retail store to arrange a shop window for: a spring-2025 Easter line received in March and April 2025 and selling down through 2026 (past collection: months of cover, sales now under 0.8 of the four weeks before), the Pikachu and unicorn plush rising through August and September, and tickets that carry both, so a bundle's evidence is in the store's own baskets


Dangerous goods and luxury assets
schema recovery: goods (UN numbers, hazard classes, packing groups; serialised watches, handbags, jewellery, wine, art), mode_rules, consignments + legs (road, rail and sea), sensor_readings, incidents, declarations, loss_claims, facilities, reverse_orders, custody_events, disposal_certificates, environmental_report, and the trade side trade_measures, trade_exposures, trade_lanes, trade_providers, trade_suppliers, trade_responses; the goods are also rows of ops.items
which hazardous and high-value shipments are at risk right now, what happened to each, the nearest facility whose licence was valid on the day, and the certificates and report rows that close the loop. Read by the connection postgres-recovery as its own role, because face_reader already sees the 40 tables a fetch sweeps in ops. See Dangerous goods and luxury assets



Late deliveries, invoices over the contracted rate and claims filed past the carrier's window occur at about 15%, 12% and 15%. About one asset in twelve has a service overdue.
Where the sites are
ops.warehouses and ops.yards give every warehouse and yard a postal address and coordinates, so a fetch of this source puts them on the twins Map: FACE writes a Site entity for each row, placed by the coordinates the row states (lat/lon on warehouses, latitude/longitude on yards), with the address and the docks of ops.docks on its page. FACE never geocodes an address: a site with only an address is listed, not placed.
The customer delivery sites (ops.customer_sites), the suppliers and the carriers' depots stand at real city centroids: the U.S. Census Bureau's 2024 Gazetteer internal point of an Illinois or Indiana city, with no street address. FACE places a destination at the coordinates the row states.
The distribution centres are authored for this quickstart, not measured. The cities, postal codes and coordinates are real places, a point in an industrial district of each city, so the Map puts each site somewhere true. No street address is a real business's.

Grade D · dataset: Files (real PDFs, images, video and sheets)
What it is
The Files dataset: the estate's documents, images, video and sheets, each laid out under the store it would live in (s3/, gcs/, azure/, sftp/, sharepoint/ and host/). It holds claim and invoice PDFs, dock photos and labels, dock video clips, a rate sheet and proof-of-delivery export, a carrier scorecard workbook, and an orders export. The connector reference is Files and object storage.
Grade
D. Dataset and model: the quickstart dataset and its expected model ship. There is no vendor system to stand up for this type; load the dataset and fetch it.
See the grade table for all 32 types.
Stand up the test system
The safety rule at the top of this page comes first: a scratch machine or a scratch cluster, never a production or platform one.

Download files.zip and unzip it. Each store has its own folder under files/: s3/, gcs/, azure/, sftp/, sharepoint/ and host/.
Put each folder where its store expects it: upload files/s3/quillmere-claims/ to a bucket named quillmere-claims in an S3-compatible store you own, served over https:// (MinIO is one open-source option), files/gcs/ to a GCS bucket, and so on.
Connect each store, in Settings › Integrations › Systems, with the connection type that reads it:

many documents under one bucket and prefix, on an S3-compatible store, GCS or a SharePoint library: a files connection, with provider naming the store;
delimited files, JSON and Parquet in a bucket, one object as a table: objectstore;
a workbook read from a path: excel;
a SharePoint list: sharepoint.

A files connection does not read the azure/, sftp/ or host/ folders: providers azure, sftp and host are refused when the connection is tested, before anything is dialled. Those folders are here as the shape of the estate's files.


The expected model
The expected model is what each file yields when it is read by its format: PDF text, an image, video frames, a sheet, or delimited text. A file is read by what it is.

Warning: The test-estate safety rule: stand the test estate up only beside a test instance, never a production deployment. Its systems are throwaway test services with published credentials: change-me is every test credential. They are still encrypted and still ask for a login, because FACE refuses a connection that is not (see Connector security). Use a scratch machine or a scratch cluster.

Grade A · dataset: Stream (a timestamped recording) · type kafka
What it is
An Apache Kafka cluster, with a Confluent-compatible Schema Registry and ksqlDB. In the test estate it is the event bus: order, shipment, reefer-alert and freight-invoice events, and the topics ksqlDB computes from them. The connector reference is Streaming: Kafka.
This page is the recording: a bounded set of records you load once. For a broker on your machine that keeps receiving the estate's sensor, drone, yard and mainframe events without end, see Apache Kafka, live estate.
Grade
A. Open source. It stands up locally from the download, with the model and its rows, end to end. Kafka is the fullest quick start: the recording holds the schemas, the Schema Registry's subjects and the records.

topics is a prefix filter: quillmere. matches all nine topics. The connection record also carries one extra setting, ksqldb_url = https://ksqldb.quillmere.invalid:8088, in config.extra. When FACE maps the estate, it reads ksqlDB through it, as well as the Schema Registry.
Credentials: password, schema_registry_password. In the test estate, every credential is change-me. Credentials are write-only: they go into the sealed credential bundle and are never returned.
Stand up the test system
The safety rule at the top of this page comes first: a scratch machine or a scratch cluster, never a production or platform one.

Stand up a broker with a SASL_SSL listener (SCRAM logins) and a Confluent-compatible Schema Registry that answers HTTPS only, with its own logins. FACE connects to nothing less. The live estate page stands up exactly that with Docker Compose, and writes the CA certificate (secrets/ca.crt) that the client configs below point at. Use a login that may create topics and produce.
Download the recording files listed under Download below. Create the nine topics, with 3 partitions each. client.properties is a Kafka client config for that listener (security.protocol=SASL_SSL, sasl.mechanism=SCRAM-SHA-512, the login and the CA):
for f in schemas/*-value.avsc; do
  kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --command-config client.properties --create --if-not-exists --topic "$(basename "$f" -value.avsc)" --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1
done


Register the subjects as the registry recording has them: every version in order, then each subject's own compatibility level. Most value schemas use TopicNameStrategy (-value). The freight invoice topic uses TopicRecordNameStrategy, and two topics also have a key subject. Set SR to your Schema Registry's https:// URL, and SR_AUTH to a registry login as user:password:
cd schema-registry
for d in subjects/*/; do
  s="$(basename "$d")"
  for v in $(jq -r '.[]' "$d/versions.json"); do
    jq '{schema, schemaType} | with_entries(select(.value != null))' "$d/versions/$v.json" \
      | curl -fsS -u "$SR_AUTH" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' --data @- "$SR/subjects/$s/versions"
  done
done
for f in config/*.json; do
  jq '{compatibility: .compatibilityLevel}' "$f" \
    | curl -fsS -u "$SR_AUTH" -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' --data @- "$SR/config/$(basename "$f" .json)"
done


Put the records on the bus. Each line of records.jsonl is one record: its topic, key and JSON value. Write one kcat file per topic, one keyvalue line per record, then produce them. kcat.conf holds the same listener settings in librdkafka form (security.protocol=SASL_SSL, sasl.mechanisms=SCRAM-SHA-512, sasl.username, sasl.password, ssl.ca.location):
mkdir -p kcat
for t in $(jq -r .topic records.jsonl | sort -u); do
  jq -r --arg t "$t" 'select(.topic == $t) | "\(.key | if type == "string" then . else tojson end)\t\(.value | tojson)"' records.jsonl > "kcat/$t.kcat"
done
for f in kcat/*.kcat; do
  kcat -F kcat.conf -P -b localhost:9092 -t "$(basename "$f" .kcat)" -K $'\t' -l "$f"
done


Add the connection in Settings › Integrations › Systems. FACE saves only a secured Kafka connection: security_protocol sasl_ssl, sasl_mechanism scram-sha-512 or scram-sha-256, a username and its password, and, when a Schema Registry is named, an https:// URL with schema_registry_username and its schema_registry_password. A broker or registry without encryption and a login is refused. The live estate page stands up a broker and registry that way and lists every setting.
Where the deployment runs ksqlDB, set the ksqldb_url extra setting. The recording's ksqldb/ folder holds the test ksqlDB's answers to LIST STREAMS EXTENDED;, LIST TABLES EXTENDED; and LIST QUERIES;, which are what FACE reads from it.

What the Schema Registry and ksqlDB add
The registry read adds metadata, not data. It sends no Fetch and no ksqlDB SELECT or PRINT. It keeps no query text and samples no value.

Schema Registry: 11 subjects. There are nine value subjects and two key subjects. Some subjects have more than one version: the shipment status and reefer alert schemas each dropped a field in version 2, and the freight invoice schema added an optional one. Every subject's compatibility level is stated. Most use the global BACKWARD, the freight invoice subject uses FULL_TRANSITIVE, and the legacy export uses NONE. Each value schema's Avro namespace names its business domain: invalid.quillmere.orders, .shipments, .coldchain or .freight.
ksqlDB: 9 sources and 4 persistent queries. ORDER_PO_DUPLICATES counts order-created events per customer PO and holds only the duplicate PO. SHIPMENT_LATEST keeps each shipment's latest status. REEFER_EXCURSIONS aggregates the reefer alerts per shipment and holds only SHP-50004. INVOICE_RATE_VARIANCE flags invoices billed more than 5% over contract and holds only INV-90003. Each query records which topic flows into which.
Traffic. ksqlDB states each source's message figures. For the legacy export, LEGACY_SHIPMENT_EXPORT, it states zero messages, and no query reads or writes it.

How the registries reduce noise in domain inference
The inference block of expected.json states what FACE's estate map infers from this connection twice: from the topic names and columns alone, and with the registry read added.

The legacy export uses the same words as the live shipment feed, so names alone place a dead topic in the shipments domain. With the registry read, ksqlDB states that the export carries no traffic, and no recorded flow ties it to a live topic, so it is withheld. The excursion table's columns (breach_count, peak_celsius, limit_celsius) share no vocabulary with the reefer alerts they are computed from, so names alone place neither topic. Their shared Avro namespace, and field docs that name the reefer alerts, put both topics in cold_chain.

Streams are dialled and held open, so their datasets are replay recordings under streams/kafka/, not a zip. Download the files, and use them as described above.
